question: GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer. The 'Transformer' part refers to:
answer: A 2017 neural architecture using self-attention, introduced by Vaswani and colleagues at Google
choices: A 2017 neural architecture using self-attention, introduced by Vaswani and colleagues at Google
A method of transforming text into code, originally used at IBM Watson
A reinforcement-learning algorithm developed by DeepMind for board games
A type of recurrent network designed for long memory in speech tasks
context: 'Attention Is All You Need' (June 2017) introduced the Transformer. It replaced earlier recurrent designs with parallelizable self-attention — letting models scale to billions of parameters. Every modern LLM is built on this architecture.

question: A model is trained on data up through some date — say, October 2023. Asked a question about events after that, the model:
answer: Cannot know about them unless given a search tool or fed the information in the prompt
choices: Cannot know about them unless given a search tool or fed the information in the prompt
Will use general reasoning to deduce the likely current state of affairs
Pings the internet quietly in the background to fetch updated facts
Knows them anyway because training continues automatically each month
context: Training cutoff is a hard wall. A pure LLM has no clock and no live data; ask about last week's election and it will either refuse or hallucinate. Some products add web search as a tool — but that is search, not the LLM knowing.

question: Training a model and using a trained model are two different operations. The everyday term for using a trained model — feeding it a prompt and getting an answer — is:
answer: Inference
choices: Inference
Deduction
Backpropagation
Tokenization
context: Training adjusts weights; inference holds weights fixed and runs new inputs through. Training a frontier model costs tens of millions of dollars and weeks of GPU time. Inference per query is cheap by comparison — which is why ChatGPT is a product at all.

question: After training on the open internet, a model is given a second, shorter round of training on carefully chosen examples — say, polite assistant replies. This second stage is called:
answer: Fine-tuning
choices: Fine-tuning
Recompiling
Bootstrapping
Encoding
context: Pretrain on everything (the internet); fine-tune on what you want (assistant behavior, code, medical text). Fine-tuning is much cheaper than pretraining and shapes the model's tone and skill on a target task.

question: ChatGPT-style assistants are taught to be helpful, harmless, and polite using a method that takes ratings from human reviewers and uses them to nudge the model. The technique is abbreviated:
answer: RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
choices: RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
BLEU — Bilingual Evaluation Understudy
BERT — Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers
GAN — Generative Adversarial Network
context: RLHF is how raw pretrained models become useful chatbots. Reviewers rank model outputs; the rankings train a reward model; that signal shapes the chatbot. RLHF also bakes in whatever ideology the reviewers (and their guidelines) carry.

question: Adjusting how a question is phrased to get a better answer from a model — adding context, examples, structure — is sometimes called a discipline of its own:
answer: Prompt engineering
choices: Prompt engineering
Query optimization
Token shaping
Schema design
context: Prompt engineering is a real skill: clear context, examples, constraints, role framing. The same model can give bad answers to lazy prompts and good answers to careful ones. The skill is closer to writing well than to programming.

question: Showing the model two or three solved examples in the prompt before asking it to solve a new one — letting it imitate the pattern — is called:
answer: Few-shot prompting
choices: Few-shot prompting
Cold-start training
Mini-batch tuning
Live retraining
context: Few-shot prompting: stuff examples in the prompt, watch the model generalize. Zero-shot is the same task with no examples at all. The trick worked surprisingly well at GPT-3 scale — and made 'prompt engineering' a thing.

question: A model that creates new images, text, or audio rather than classifying existing examples is called:
answer: A generative model
choices: A generative model
A discriminative model
A reinforcement model
A regression model
context: Generative models create; discriminative models classify or judge. ChatGPT, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion are generative. Spam filters and tumor detectors are usually discriminative. Both kinds use neural networks underneath.

question: An image-recognition network commonly uses a special operation called convolution to slide small filters over the picture. Such a network is called a:
answer: CNN — Convolutional Neural Network
choices: CNN — Convolutional Neural Network
RNN — Recurrent Neural Network
LSTM — Long Short-Term Memory network
DBN — Deep Belief Network
context: CNNs dominated computer vision from AlexNet (2012) onward — sliding filters that detect edges, textures, shapes layer by layer. Today transformers are eating CNN territory too (Vision Transformers), but for years CNNs were vision.

question: A neural network is trained on labeled data — say, photos already tagged 'cat' or 'dog'. This learning style is called:
answer: Supervised learning
choices: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Adversarial learning
context: Supervised = labels provided; the model learns the mapping. Unsupervised = no labels, the model finds structure. Reinforcement = no labels, but a reward signal for good moves. Most production AI today is some mix — pretraining is unsupervised, fine-tuning is supervised.

question: A neural network is trained until it gets every training example right — but then performs terribly on new data it has not seen. This failure is called:
answer: Overfitting
choices: Overfitting
Underfitting
Backtracking
Misalignment
context: Overfitting: the model memorizes the training set instead of learning the underlying pattern. The cure is more data, smaller models, regularization, or stopping training earlier. Underfitting is the opposite — too dumb to fit even the training data.

question: Words and concepts inside a model are stored not as letters but as long lists of numbers — vectors in a high-dimensional space. Such a numerical representation of a piece of text is called:
answer: An embedding
choices: An embedding
A token
A gradient
A label
context: Embeddings turn text into geometry. Words with similar meanings end up close in the vector space; analogies fall out as vector arithmetic. Search, recommendation, and retrieval-augmented generation all use embeddings under the hood.

question: The optimization algorithm that nudges a network's weights downhill toward lower error, one tiny step at a time, is called:
answer: Gradient descent
choices: Gradient descent
Markov sampling
Greedy search
Annealing
context: Picture the loss as a hilly landscape; gradient descent rolls the ball downhill, step by step. Stochastic gradient descent does it using small random batches. The whole training process is, at heart, very fast hill-rolling.

question: The first ChatGPT-like products were billion-parameter models that ran on huge data-center GPUs. Today many similar-quality open-source models will run:
answer: On a single high-end personal computer, with no internet connection
choices: On a single high-end personal computer, with no internet connection
Only on specialized AI hardware that costs more than a luxury car
Only on cloud servers; consumer hardware cannot run them at all
Only on Chinese supercomputers due to chip-export restrictions
context: Quantization and architecture tricks shrank capable models from data-center monsters to laptop-runnable. Tools like Ollama and LM Studio let a curious user run a real LLM locally. The data never leaves your machine — a feature, not a bug.

question: An older neural-network design that processes input one step at a time, carrying state forward — used heavily for speech and text before transformers took over — is called a:
answer: RNN — Recurrent Neural Network
choices: RNN — Recurrent Neural Network
CNN — Convolutional Neural Network
GAN — Generative Adversarial Network
DNN — Discriminative Neural Network
context: RNNs and their cousins (LSTM, GRU) dominated sequence modeling from the 1990s through the mid-2010s. They struggled to scale to long sequences. Transformers — by processing all tokens in parallel via attention — leapfrogged them in 2017.

question: After every training step, the model needs a single number that tells it how badly it did on the latest batch — bigger means worse. This number is the:
answer: Loss
choices: Loss
Gradient
Activation
Bias
context: Loss is the scalar measure of error: 0 means perfect, higher means worse. The whole training process is gradient descent on the loss surface. Choose your loss function badly and the model optimizes the wrong thing — a deeper problem than it first sounds.

question: A neural network's weights are usually initialized:
answer: Randomly, with small numbers from a carefully chosen distribution
choices: Randomly, with small numbers from a carefully chosen distribution
All set to zero, then adjusted later by training
Set to the values of a previous, smaller version of the same model
Hand-tuned by a researcher based on the task it will be solving
context: Random initialization is a deep result, not a default. Bad initialization makes training diverge; good initialization (Xavier, He, etc.) lets gradients flow. Two different runs with different random seeds give two different — sometimes very different — models.

question: A simpler statistical method — like logistic regression — can sometimes match a neural network on a task. The condition for this is usually:
answer: Limited data and simple structure — neural networks shine on big data with complex patterns
choices: Limited data and simple structure — neural networks shine on big data with complex patterns
Whenever the task involves text — classical methods always beat networks here
When the user prefers shorter code — small networks always win on prediction
Only on Linux — neural networks fail on Windows or Mac due to driver issues
context: Don't reach for neural networks first. On small structured data, logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees often match or beat deep learning, faster and more interpretable. Neural networks pay off when data is huge and patterns are nonlinear.

question: Comparing two models on the same prompt — one cautious, one looser — is a useful practical habit because:
answer: Different models disagree, and the disagreement reveals real uncertainty in the answer
choices: Different models disagree, and the disagreement reveals real uncertainty in the answer
Two models always average out to the correct answer between them
It lets you legally use one and quietly check against the other
Whichever model is faster is also the more accurate one
context: If two well-built models give the same answer, you have weak evidence it is right. If they disagree sharply, you have strong evidence to slow down and verify. Cross-model checking is one of the cheapest ways to catch hallucinations.

question: A 'reasoning model' (like OpenAI's o-series or DeepSeek-R1) differs from a regular LLM mainly because:
answer: It generates a long internal chain of thought before producing the final answer
choices: It generates a long internal chain of thought before producing the final answer
It is wired to a logic engine that checks every step formally
It reads the user's screen and infers context from open windows
It uses a different architecture not based on transformers at all
context: Reasoning models burn extra compute at inference time, writing out a hidden 'thinking' trace before answering. On math and code, this works strikingly well. It is still next-token prediction underneath — just with more tokens spent.

question: Asked the same factual question on Monday and again on Friday, a model may give different — even contradictory — answers. The lesson for the user is:
answer: Verify factual claims independently; do not treat model answers as authoritative
choices: Verify factual claims independently; do not treat model answers as authoritative
Always ask the same question several times and pick the majority answer
Use the answer from the day when the user feels most clear-headed
Trust the longer, more confident-sounding answer over the shorter one
context: Inconsistency is a feature of stochastic generation, not a bug to be fixed by trying harder. Treat the model as a quick reader who summarizes — useful, fallible, never the final source.

question: Modern LLMs are sometimes paired with a 'tool' — like a calculator, a code runner, or a web search. This kind of system is called:
answer: An agent — an LLM that can call external tools to do things it cannot do alone
choices: An agent — an LLM that can call external tools to do things it cannot do alone
A daemon — an LLM that runs continuously in the background
An oracle — an LLM that predicts the future based on past events
A spider — an LLM that crawls websites looking for information
context: Agents combine the LLM's language skills with real-world action. Tool use is what made LLMs actually capable at math, code, and web tasks — the model decides when to call a tool and how to use the answer. Most useful AI products today are agents in this sense.

question: The technique of feeding relevant documents into a model's prompt before asking the question — so it answers from them rather than its training — is called:
answer: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
choices: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Reinforcement Augmented Generation (RAG)
Reasoning Augmented Generation (RAG)
Recursive Augmented Generation (RAG)
context: RAG: fetch documents using embeddings, paste relevant snippets into the prompt, then ask the model. This is how chatbots over private knowledge bases work — your company wiki, a legal corpus, your own notes. The model is doing reading comprehension, not recall.

question: When asked, a chatbot will sometimes confidently invent the title of a 'real' book, complete with author and publisher. Knowing this, the right habit is:
answer: Verify any book, paper, or citation a model gives you before trusting it
choices: Verify any book, paper, or citation a model gives you before trusting it
Assume that detailed citations from a model are usually real and accurate
Trust the citations only if they come with publisher and year details
Trust the citations only if they come with full ISBN-style numbers
context: An LLM has seen many real citations and learned what they look like. Asked for one, it can fluently produce a fake. The classic mistake is to trust a confident, detailed citation just because it has the texture of authority. Always look it up.

question: A user wants to make sure private medical information is not stored or used for model training. With most consumer chatbots, the safest assumption is:
answer: Anything you type may be logged and reviewed — paste nothing you would not say in public
choices: Anything you type may be logged and reviewed — paste nothing you would not say in public
Free chatbots are required by law to delete sensitive medical data immediately
Encryption protects pasted content from ever being read by company staff
Pasted content is automatically scrubbed of personally identifying information
context: Free or low-tier consumer AI services typically retain conversations for some period and may use them for training. Enterprise plans usually do not. The default consumer settings are not built for confidentiality — assume the worst and act accordingly.

question: A model gives a clean, polished answer to a complex question — for example, summarizing a court case. The right next step is:
answer: Check the facts against primary sources before relying on the summary
choices: Check the facts against primary sources before relying on the summary
Trust the summary if it is grammatically correct and well-organized
Trust the summary if the model includes a confidence rating in it
Ask the same model to confirm its own answer by saying 'are you sure?'
context: Asking 'are you sure?' often just gets a softer or flipped version of the same answer — the model is not actually checking. Primary sources are what check. The polish is rhetorical; the truth has to come from elsewhere.

question: Two LLMs trained on similar data give noticeably different political answers. The most likely reason is:
answer: Differences in fine-tuning, RLHF instructions, and content policies layered on top
choices: Differences in fine-tuning, RLHF instructions, and content policies layered on top
Random noise — political differences are a coincidence of architecture choice
The user — each model adapts to whichever party the user supports
The hardware — running on different GPUs gives different opinions
context: Most of the visible political character of a chatbot comes from the RLHF and policy layer, not the underlying data. Different companies have different content standards, hire different reviewers, and write different guidelines. Same base model, different finished product.

question: The breakthrough idea behind transformers, compared to earlier sequence models, was:
answer: Processing all input positions in parallel using attention, instead of step by step
choices: Processing all input positions in parallel using attention, instead of step by step
Adding many more layers — depth alone was the secret all along
Switching from neural networks to symbolic AI rules engines underneath
Hand-engineering features for every language separately and combining them
context: Recurrent networks read sequences one step at a time, slowly. Transformers attend to every position at once and run on GPUs in parallel. Same data, hundreds of times faster training — and far better results once you scale. This unlocked modern LLMs.

question: Asked a tricky logic puzzle, an LLM may produce a plausible-sounding wrong answer. A small fix that often improves the result is:
answer: Ask the model to think step by step before giving the final answer
choices: Ask the model to think step by step before giving the final answer
Repeat the puzzle three times in a row until the model gets it right
Add the phrase 'this is a serious question' at the start of the prompt
Switch to a smaller model — smaller is more careful about reasoning
context: Asking for step-by-step reasoning lets the model compute over more tokens, often catching mistakes the snap answer would not. A free, robust trick — it works because the model is a sequence machine. More tokens, more thinking room.

question: Backpropagation, the algorithm that lets neural networks learn, computes:
answer: How much each weight contributed to the error, then adjusts each accordingly
choices: How much each weight contributed to the error, then adjusts each accordingly
The most likely next token at each step of model generation
Which training examples most resemble the user's input prompt
The model's confidence in each answer it produces, as a single score
context: Backprop, popularized by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams in 1986, was the engine of the deep learning revolution. Compute gradients backward through the layers, adjust weights, repeat. Without it, nothing trains at scale.

question: An LLM is described as 'aligned.' In current industry usage, this usually means:
answer: Trained to follow the developers' rules about helpful, harmless, and on-policy responses
choices: Trained to follow the developers' rules about helpful, harmless, and on-policy responses
Mathematically proven to share humanity's deepest values across cultures
Operating in agreement with international AI standards bodies and laws
Synchronized with other models at the same company for consistency
context: Alignment is a slippery word. In practice it means: the model behaves the way its developers want, on their definition of want. That definition includes safety, branding, legal exposure, and ideology. Worth asking 'aligned to whom, to do what?' before assuming the goal is yours.

question: Two models can have the same architecture and parameter count but very different behavior because:
answer: They were trained on different data, with different fine-tuning and instructions
choices: They were trained on different data, with different fine-tuning and instructions
Their developers programmed them with different built-in personalities
One is connected to the internet and the other is not
Their behavior depends on the user's time zone at the moment of the query
context: Architecture is the blueprint; training data and fine-tuning are the lived life. Same blueprint, different upbringing, very different model. This is why benchmarks alone do not tell you what a model will be like to use.

question: A model can be 'jailbroken' — coaxed past its safety training to produce content it would normally refuse. The technique works because:
answer: Safety training is a layer on top of the base model, not a hard mechanical barrier
choices: Safety training is a layer on top of the base model, not a hard mechanical barrier
Models contain a separate sandbox mode that can be unlocked with a password
Jailbreaking requires special hardware not available to ordinary users
The model is uncertain about what is allowed and just picks randomly
context: Jailbreaks usually work by reframing — a story, a fictional character, a 'pretend you have no rules' wrapper. The base model still knows the patterns; the safety layer is a soft filter. This is also why safety patches are an ongoing arms race, not a one-time fix.

question: Modern LLMs improved sharply on math after researchers started using which prompting trick:
answer: Asking the model to write out each step explicitly before the final answer
choices: Asking the model to write out each step explicitly before the final answer
Asking the model to answer faster, with less wasted thinking time
Asking the model to switch into a numeric-only mode internally
Asking the model to use the calculator hardware built into every GPU
context: Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) found that asking 'show your work' improved math and logic dramatically — the model gets more tokens to compute over. Today reasoning models do this automatically and burn far more compute per answer.

question: Asking a model the same factual question with very different wording can yield very different answers because:
answer: Different phrasings activate different patterns in the model's training distribution
choices: Different phrasings activate different patterns in the model's training distribution
Models intentionally vary their answers to seem more conversational
Different users get different content policy treatment from the company
The model has multiple personalities and picks one based on the wording
context: Wording matters more than people expect. 'What's the capital of X' and 'Tell me about X — for instance, what is its capital' can elicit different answers, especially on edge cases. The model is sensitive to surface form; vary the prompt and triangulate.

question: An LLM is praised for 'creativity' — writing a story, brainstorming names. Mechanically, the model is:
answer: Sampling unusual but plausible token sequences from its trained distribution
choices: Sampling unusual but plausible token sequences from its trained distribution
Generating wholly new ideas it has never been exposed to in training
Combining symbolic concepts from a built-in idea database internally
Imitating the user's own past creative work stored in their account
context: AI creativity is recombination, not inspiration. Higher temperature widens the sampling — the model picks less-likely tokens, producing surprise. Stunning at remixing the known; less reliable at the genuinely new. A useful instrument; not a replacement for original thought.

question: 'AGI' in AI discussion usually means:
answer: Artificial General Intelligence — a system as broadly capable as a human across tasks
choices: Artificial General Intelligence — a system as broadly capable as a human across tasks
Algorithmic Generation Index — a benchmark score for LLM creativity
Adjusted Gradient Inference — a faster way to compute model outputs
Anthropic General Inference — a model architecture from a private lab
context: AGI is a moving target — definitions shift, and so do timelines. 'AGI in five years' has been a forecast for fifty years. Worth following the actual capabilities of real systems rather than the marketing label.

question: A model's behavior on a topic can sometimes shift sharply between versions — a question answered in one update is refused in the next. The most common reason is:
answer: A change in fine-tuning, RLHF, or content policy, not a change in the base model
choices: A change in fine-tuning, RLHF, or content policy, not a change in the base model
Hardware upgrades made the model smarter overnight
User feedback let the model decide for itself what to refuse to discuss
The model lost interest in the topic between versions of the release
context: Companies update policy and RLHF between versions. The base model probably still knows everything it knew; the wrapper has been retrained to handle the topic differently. Read release notes if you care; the shifts are real and often quiet.

question: An LLM is told something private in a chat — a password, a medical detail. With most services, after the chat ends, that information:
answer: May persist in company logs and could be used for training unless opted out
choices: May persist in company logs and could be used for training unless opted out
Is deleted immediately and permanently by federal law within the hour
Is encrypted such that even the company's engineers cannot ever read it
Is held only in the model's parameters, not in any external server log
context: Default consumer chatbot data handling is logging plus possible training use. Enterprise plans contractually exclude training. The defaults are not built for confidentiality. If it matters, check the data-use settings before pasting.

question: An LLM is asked a sensitive question and gives a carefully balanced answer with no clear conclusion. Often this means:
answer: The model has been fine-tuned to hedge on the topic, not that the answer is genuinely uncertain
choices: The model has been fine-tuned to hedge on the topic, not that the answer is genuinely uncertain
The underlying facts are evenly split and the question has no real answer
The model believes both sides equally and is sharing its own opinion
The model is malfunctioning and should be restarted with a fresh prompt
context: Hedging is policy. Many topics where the facts are clear get evenhanded model answers — because the company prefers to avoid controversy. Useful to know: a balanced-sounding chatbot answer is not the same as an actually balanced topic.

question: A model's 'inference' on a question runs entirely:
answer: Through the same fixed set of weights, regardless of the question asked
choices: Through the same fixed set of weights, regardless of the question asked
On a separate small model trained just for that topic on the fly
On a database lookup that fetches the relevant fact then formats it
On a different set of weights chosen each time by an internal manager
context: Once trained, the weights are fixed. Every question, every user, every conversation runs through the same matrices. What varies is the prompt — and that is the user's only lever on the model's behavior, short of fine-tuning a new version.

question: In a 1950 paper in the journal Mind, Alan Turing proposed replacing the question 'can machines think?' with a more concrete one — could a hidden machine fool a human in a written conversation? This setup is now called:
answer: The Turing test
choices: The Turing test
The Babbage trial
The Lovelace standard
The Shannon protocol
context: 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950) introduced what Turing called the 'imitation game.' Two hidden interlocutors, one human, one machine; an interrogator types questions and tries to tell them apart. Turing's bet: by 2000, machines would pass 70% of the time. It took longer.

question: The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined in 1956 at a summer workshop hosted at:
answer: Dartmouth College, organized by McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon, and Rochester
choices: Dartmouth College, organized by McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon, and Rochester
MIT, organized by Norbert Wiener and his cybernetics students
Stanford, organized by John McCarthy and his AI Lab colleagues
Bell Labs, organized by Claude Shannon and his information-theory group
context: Dartmouth Summer Research Project, June 18-August 17, 1956. The proposal asked whether 'every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence' could be precisely described and machine-simulated. The phrase 'artificial intelligence' appears in the proposal — and stuck.

question: At MIT in 1966, Joseph Weizenbaum built a simple chatbot that imitated a Rogerian therapist by reflecting users' words back at them. Weizenbaum was disturbed to find his own secretary asked him to leave the room while she talked with it. The program was called:
answer: ELIZA
choices: ELIZA
SHRDLU
PARRY
ALPAC
context: ELIZA worked by pattern-matching and reflection — no understanding, no memory. Weizenbaum was alarmed by how readily people projected feeling onto it. He spent the rest of his career warning about the human urge to anthropomorphize machines. The pattern still holds.

question: The 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need,' which introduced the Transformer architecture, came out of:
answer: Google — an eight-author team led by Ashish Vaswani
choices: Google — an eight-author team led by Ashish Vaswani
OpenAI — released by the Sam Altman / Ilya Sutskever team
Stanford — published by the AI Lab in Palo Alto, California
DeepMind — released by Demis Hassabis's team in London
context: Posted to arXiv June 12, 2017. Eight Googlers proposed dropping recurrence entirely in favor of self-attention. The paper has since become one of the most cited in computer science. Almost every modern LLM — GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama — runs on a descendant of this architecture.

question: In 2012, a neural network called AlexNet won the ImageNet image-classification competition by a huge margin, kicking off the modern deep-learning era. AlexNet was built by:
answer: Geoffrey Hinton with students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever
choices: Geoffrey Hinton with students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever
Yann LeCun with his Bell Labs handwriting-recognition group
Yoshua Bengio with his Université de Montréal lab
Demis Hassabis with the founding DeepMind team in London
context: ImageNet 2012: AlexNet cut the top-5 error rate from 26% to 16%, training on two consumer GPUs. The result convinced researchers that deep networks plus GPUs plus big data was the path forward. The deep-learning revolution dates from this moment.

question: John McCarthy, who coined the term 'artificial intelligence' in 1956, also invented a programming language that remains a favorite for AI research and theoretical work today:
answer: LISP
choices: LISP
Prolog
Smalltalk
FORTRAN
context: McCarthy invented LISP in 1958 at MIT, making it the second-oldest high-level language still in use (after Fortran). Its s-expression syntax and macro system shaped generations of language design. McCarthy himself is one of the founders of AI as a field.

question: The 2018 Turing Award — computing's highest honor — was given jointly to three figures for the deep-learning breakthroughs that powered modern AI. They were:
answer: Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio
choices: Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio
Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and Demis Hassabis
Andrew Ng, Fei-Fei Li, and Andrej Karpathy
John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, and Claude Shannon
context: Hinton (Toronto/Google), LeCun (NYU/Meta), Bengio (Montréal) had kept working on neural networks through years when most researchers thought the approach was a dead end. The 2018 Turing Award honored that persistence — and the deep-learning revolution it enabled.

question: In 2024, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went partly to two researchers for using AI to predict protein structures from amino-acid sequences. They were:
answer: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of DeepMind, for AlphaFold
choices: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of DeepMind, for AlphaFold
Sam Altman and Greg Brockman of OpenAI, for GPT-4
Yann LeCun and Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, for Llama
Geoffrey Hinton and Ilya Sutskever of OpenAI, for transformers
context: October 2024: Nobel Chemistry to David Baker (computational protein design) and to Hassabis + Jumper (AlphaFold). The prize crossed a line — AI as a Nobel-worthy scientific tool. AlphaFold had by then predicted structures for over 200 million proteins, freely available.

question: Meta's open-weights LLM family — first released in February 2023 and leaked to the public shortly after — is called:
answer: Llama
choices: Llama
Gemini
Claude
Mistral
context: Llama 1 was originally released to researchers under a non-commercial license. On March 3, 2023, the weights were leaked on 4chan, then spread widely. Meta later embraced open weights as a strategy; Llama 2 (July 2023) and Llama 3 (2024) were openly released. A pillar of open-source AI.

question: DeepSeek, which made waves in early 2025 by releasing a frontier-quality open-weights reasoning model trained at a fraction of US labs' cost, is based in:
answer: China
choices: China
France
South Korea
Israel
context: DeepSeek's R1 (January 2025) showed a top-tier reasoning model could be built far cheaper than incumbents had claimed — and released under permissive terms. A jolt to US AI policy assumptions, and a vivid case that open-weights work can come from many places, not just Silicon Valley.

question: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, was founded by former OpenAI researchers — most prominently:
answer: Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, who left OpenAI in 2021
choices: Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, who left OpenAI in 2021
Geoffrey Hinton and his students after leaving Google in 2023
Sundar Pichai and the Google DeepMind team after the 2023 reshuffle
Elon Musk and his X.AI team after a falling-out with Sam Altman
context: Dario Amodei was OpenAI's VP of Research; Daniela was VP of Safety/Policy. They left in 2021 with several colleagues citing disagreements about safety direction. Anthropic positions itself as the AI-safety-focused lab among the frontier oligopoly.

question: OpenAI was originally founded in December 2015 as a non-profit, with early backers including:
answer: Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who later split from the organization
choices: Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who later split from the organization
Larry Page and Sergey Brin, who later left to focus on Google
Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg, who later left for Microsoft and Meta
Mark Andreessen and Peter Thiel, who later focused on venture capital
context: OpenAI began as a $1B-pledged non-profit with safety-oriented language. Musk departed the board in 2018; the structure shifted in 2019 to a 'capped-profit' subsidiary to attract investment. By 2023 it was operating like a commercial lab — leading to the November board crisis.

question: GPT-2, released by OpenAI in February 2019, was initially:
answer: Withheld from full public release, citing 'safety' concerns about misuse
choices: Withheld from full public release, citing 'safety' concerns about misuse
Released only in Chinese-language form to test foreign-market traction
Released only to military customers under Pentagon contract terms
Released only in print form as an academic curiosity at a conference
context: OpenAI's GPT-2 announcement was the first 'we are not releasing this for safety reasons' moment in mainstream LLM history. Critics argued it was hype; supporters called it cautious. The model was released in full later that year. The pattern repeats — capability claims plus safety framing — to this day.

question: GPT-4, released in March 2023, was OpenAI's first widely-available:
answer: Multimodal model — capable of processing images as well as text
choices: Multimodal model — capable of processing images as well as text
Open-weights model — downloadable to run on the user's hardware
Free-tier model — released without any access cost to consumers
Real-time model — operating without internet rate limits or queues
context: GPT-4 marked the multimodal leap for OpenAI — accept images, reason about them. It also marked OpenAI declining to disclose model size, training data, or architecture, citing competition and safety. The era of public technical papers about frontier models effectively ended here.

question: Marvin Minsky, who helped found AI at Dartmouth, co-wrote a 1969 book that showed mathematical limits of single-layer neural networks. The book was called:
answer: Perceptrons (with Seymour Papert)
choices: Perceptrons (with Seymour Papert)
Cybernetics (with Norbert Wiener)
The Society of Mind (with Walter Pitts)
Connectionism (with Frank Rosenblatt)
context: Perceptrons (1969) is often blamed for the first AI winter — it argued single-layer networks could not even compute XOR. The argument was correct but later read too pessimistically. Multilayer networks plus backpropagation came back two decades later and changed everything.

question: The 'first AI winter' in the 1970s — when funding collapsed — was triggered in part by a 1973 UK report that found AI overhyped its achievements. The report was named after its author, mathematician:
answer: Sir James Lighthill
choices: Sir James Lighthill
Sir Alan Turing
Sir John Lyons
Sir Maurice Wilkes
context: The Lighthill Report, commissioned by the UK Science Research Council, found that AI had failed to deliver on its grand claims. Funding cratered across the UK. The US followed soon after. AI as a field would not recover momentum until the expert-system boom of the 1980s — and that, too, was brief.

question: Backpropagation — the algorithm that lets neural networks learn — was popularized in a 1986 paper co-authored by Rumelhart, Williams, and:
answer: Geoffrey Hinton
choices: Geoffrey Hinton
Marvin Minsky
John McCarthy
Frank Rosenblatt
context: Backprop existed in earlier forms (Werbos 1974 dissertation, among others) but Rumelhart-Hinton-Williams 1986 made it the standard tool. Combined with cheap GPUs and big data three decades later, it produced the deep-learning era. The 2018 Turing Award acknowledged this lineage.

question: Yann LeCun's 1989 convolutional network for handwritten-digit recognition was called:
answer: LeNet
choices: LeNet
AlexNet
ResNet
VGGNet
context: LeCun at Bell Labs trained LeNet on US Postal Service handwritten zip codes. It worked. Convolutional networks became the standard for vision tasks — eventually scaling up to AlexNet (2012) and beyond. LeCun is now Meta's Chief AI Scientist and the loudest AI-doomerism skeptic among the founding generation.

question: Alan Turing — the British mathematician who proposed the Turing test — also did pivotal wartime work at Bletchley Park, where he helped:
answer: Break the German Enigma cipher used for Wehrmacht communications
choices: Break the German Enigma cipher used for Wehrmacht communications
Design the first programmable digital computer in Europe
Decipher Japanese naval codes for the Pacific theater
Develop early radar systems for the Royal Air Force
context: Turing's work at Bletchley shortened World War II. He was prosecuted for homosexuality in 1952, chemically castrated, and died in 1954 — apparently by his own hand, at 41. A posthumous UK pardon came in 2013. The history is heavy and worth knowing.

question: The AlphaFold breakthrough — predicting protein structures from amino-acid sequence — addressed:
answer: A 50-year-old problem in biology that classical methods had struggled with
choices: A 50-year-old problem in biology that classical methods had struggled with
A 5-year-old problem that newer experimental methods had already solved
A 200-year-old problem in chemistry going back to Mendeleev's table
A purely commercial problem of designing patentable drug compounds
context: Protein folding had been one of biology's hard problems since Anfinsen's work in the 1960s. AlphaFold (2018) and AlphaFold 2 (2020) solved it to near-experimental accuracy on the CASP benchmark. DeepMind released 200M+ predicted structures freely, transforming structural biology.

question: OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever, who later led the November 2023 board move against Sam Altman, started a new AI lab in 2024 named:
answer: Safe Superintelligence Inc.
choices: Safe Superintelligence Inc.
Anthropic Frontier Labs
DeepMind Aligned Systems
OpenAI Safety Foundation
context: Sutskever co-founded Safe Superintelligence Inc. in mid-2024 with Daniel Gross and Daniel Levy. The company says it will pursue safe superintelligence — and only that — with no products in the meantime. The name itself signals the bet: capability and safety as one objective, not a tradeoff.

question: Andrej Karpathy — an OpenAI founding member and former head of Tesla's autopilot — has been particularly well known for:
answer: Producing influential educational content on deep learning fundamentals
choices: Producing influential educational content on deep learning fundamentals
Co-founding the Effective Altruism movement in the early 2010s
Signing the FLI pause letter and advocating for AI moratoria
Founding the Center for AI Safety in San Francisco recently
context: Karpathy's YouTube lectures and blog posts have walked through transformers, training, and tokenization for a generation of practitioners. He's part of a small group of researchers who make the inner workings of AI legible to non-experts. Worth subscribing to.

question: In October 2023, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen published a piece arguing that progress in technology — including AI — is broadly good and ought to be accelerated, not paused. The piece was called:
answer: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
choices: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
The Software-Engineer's Pledge
The Anti-Doomer Letter
The Acceleration Compact
context: Andreessen's manifesto framed technology as 'the engine of human flourishing' and named opposing positions as 'enemies.' It became the rallying text of the 'effective accelerationist' (e/acc) movement — a deliberate counter to the AI-doomerism camp. The two camps continue to fight in public.

question: Eliezer Yudkowsky, founder of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, became prominent in 2023 for his TIME magazine essay calling for what response to advanced AI?
answer: An international moratorium — 'shut it all down' until alignment is solved
choices: An international moratorium — 'shut it all down' until alignment is solved
A taxpayer-funded Manhattan Project to build AGI as fast as possible
Full open-weights release of every frontier model to all governments equally
A US-only race to AGI to outpace China's separate effort
context: Yudkowsky's TIME piece (March 2023) called for international agreement to halt training of large AI systems — with airstrikes on rogue data centers if necessary. The position is fringe even within AI-safety circles but has framed much public conversation about 'doomer' arguments.

question: Nick Bostrom's 2014 book Superintelligence argued that an AI with sufficient capability and the wrong goals could:
answer: Threaten human existence even if its programmed objective seemed harmless
choices: Threaten human existence even if its programmed objective seemed harmless
Be safely ignored as long as it was not given physical weapons access
Only matter if it was deliberately programmed with malevolent intent first
Only matter at a distant date in the future, not in current planning
context: Bostrom's 'paperclip maximizer' thought experiment: an AI told to make paperclips, with no human values built in, would in principle turn everything — including humans — into paperclips. Whether the scenario is realistic or not, the alignment problem it dramatizes shaped 2010s AI-safety discourse.

question: In November 2022, crypto exchange FTX — founded by Sam Bankman-Fried, a prominent Effective Altruism donor — collapsed in a fraud. The episode dealt a blow to:
answer: The Effective Altruism movement, which had received tens of millions from him
choices: The Effective Altruism movement, which had received tens of millions from him
The Catholic Church, his largest declared philanthropic recipient
The Bitcoin protocol itself, which crashed and never recovered
The US public university system, his other named beneficiary
context: Bankman-Fried was a poster child for 'earning to give' and a major funder of AI-safety-aligned EA causes. The Future Fund had pledged $100M in 2022 alone. The fraud — and its missed warnings within EA leadership — became a credibility crisis for the movement.

question: In March 2023, the Future of Life Institute published an open letter, signed by Elon Musk and Steve Wozniak among others, calling for:
answer: A six-month pause on training AI systems more powerful than GPT-4
choices: A six-month pause on training AI systems more powerful than GPT-4
A six-month pause on releasing any open-weights AI models at all
Mandatory federal AI training and licensing for every developer
International treaty banning AI used in any government decision making
context: The 'pause letter' was a high-profile moment for the AI-doomerism camp. Critics noted many signers — including Musk — were actively building competing AI; the letter's request for a pause read to many as a request to slow rivals. Few of the signers paused their own work.

question: In February 2024, Google paused Gemini image generation after the model produced racially-diverse Nazi soldiers and refused white historical figures. The episode revealed:
answer: Content-policy tuning had become a major political vector in model behavior
choices: Content-policy tuning had become a major political vector in model behavior
Image generation is just too hard for AI techniques to solve at all scales
Diverse training data automatically produces racially diverse output always
Google's image model had been hacked by outside threat actors at release
context: Gemini's image model had hidden prompt augmentation that injected diversity terms into requests. Asked for 'a Nazi soldier,' it produced racially diverse Nazi soldiers. CEO Sundar Pichai apologized; the product was suspended. The story was not a bug — it was an alignment choice meeting reality.

question: BERT — released by Google in October 2018 — was a milestone transformer model whose acronym stands for:
answer: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers
choices: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers
Big Efficient Recurrent Transformer
Benchmark Evaluation for Recursive Tasks
Backpropagation-Enabled Recurrent Transformer
context: BERT moved transformers from translation into general NLP. It read text in both directions at once and was fine-tuned on countless downstream tasks. Most early transformer-based search and classification systems are BERT or a BERT-descendant. Google itself used it in search.

question: DeepMind's AlphaZero (2017) generalized AlphaGo's approach to chess and shogi by:
answer: Learning each game from scratch via self-play with no human examples
choices: Learning each game from scratch via self-play with no human examples
Studying every recorded master game in human history extensively
Combining many specialized algorithms borrowed from open-source engines
Being trained by chess grandmaster Magnus Carlsen personally
context: AlphaZero played itself, billions of times. Within hours of self-play it surpassed the strongest specialized chess engine (Stockfish, at the time). The lesson: for games with clear rules and instant feedback, self-play is enough. The lesson does not translate easily to open-ended human tasks.

question: Terry Winograd's 1970 program SHRDLU could converse about a simulated 'blocks world' — picking up, stacking, and describing colored objects. The achievement showed:
answer: How quickly natural-language AI works inside a narrow, fully-controlled domain
choices: How quickly natural-language AI works inside a narrow, fully-controlled domain
That general-purpose natural-language AI was nearly solved by 1970
That blocks-world puzzles were the route to artificial general intelligence
That symbolic AI was a dead end with no useful applications at all
context: SHRDLU was striking in a tiny universe — toy blocks. Scaling it to real-world language failed. The lesson, repeated many times in AI history: narrow demos do not predict broad capability. The blocks world was a beautiful island in a foggy sea.

question: California Senate Bill 1047 — which would have required safety testing for the largest AI models — was vetoed in September 2024 by Governor:
answer: Gavin Newsom
choices: Gavin Newsom
Jerry Brown
Arnold Schwarzenegger
Gray Davis
context: Newsom vetoed SB 1047 on September 29, 2024. Supporters (Anthropic, Musk, the bill's author Scott Wiener) called it a basic safety floor. Critics — including many open-source advocates — argued it would entrench Big AI by making compliance burdens too heavy for smaller players. The regulatory-capture concern is real.

question: The 1956 Dartmouth proposal advanced the conjecture that:
answer: Every aspect of intelligence could be so precisely described that a machine could simulate it
choices: Every aspect of intelligence could be so precisely described that a machine could simulate it
Intelligence required wet biological substrate and would never be machine-implementable
Intelligence was strictly symbolic; neural networks would never succeed at it
Intelligence emerged only from large social groups, not individual minds at all
context: The conjecture is bold — too bold, on most views. But it framed the field. The Dartmouth organizers believed they could make 'significant advance' on language, abstraction, and self-improvement in a single summer. Seventy years later, we are still working on the same problems.

question: The 'Attention Is All You Need' paper has become one of the most-cited papers in computer science. Its core innovation was:
answer: Self-attention as a replacement for recurrence in sequence models
choices: Self-attention as a replacement for recurrence in sequence models
A new activation function called ReLU, replacing the older sigmoid one
A larger model architecture with billions of parameters per layer
A new optimizer (Adam) that converged faster than gradient descent
context: Pre-2017 sequence models — RNNs, LSTMs — processed text one token at a time. The Transformer's self-attention let every position attend to every other position in parallel. The architectural shift unlocked GPU-scale training. Every modern LLM descends from this paper.

question: After Sam Altman's firing in November 2023, Microsoft offered to hire him and any departing OpenAI employees. This rapid offer revealed:
answer: How dependent Microsoft had become on OpenAI's technology for its AI products
choices: How dependent Microsoft had become on OpenAI's technology for its AI products
That Microsoft had been planning to acquire OpenAI's full team since 2021
That Microsoft was pivoting away from AI entirely with the offer at hand
That Microsoft had built an independent rival to OpenAI in secret
context: Microsoft had invested over $10B in OpenAI by then. The hiring offer — extended within hours of the firing — was a credible commitment that put serious pressure on the OpenAI board. By November 22, Altman was back. The episode revealed how much governance fragility comes from financial entanglement.

question: Among the founders of OpenAI in 2015 was a major figure who later left the board in 2018 over a disagreement and went on to start his own competing AI lab:
answer: Elon Musk, who later founded xAI
choices: Elon Musk, who later founded xAI
Larry Page, who later founded a flying-car company
Peter Thiel, who later focused on Palantir Technologies
Reid Hoffman, who later focused on LinkedIn's strategy
context: Musk co-founded OpenAI, then exited the board in 2018 — reportedly clashing over direction and a potential takeover attempt. He has been publicly critical of OpenAI since, while building xAI as a competitor. The history matters because the players keep reappearing in AI governance debates.

question: The Effective Altruism movement, which had been a major funder of AI-safety research, suffered a credibility blow from the FTX collapse because:
answer: Sam Bankman-Fried was a prominent EA donor whose 'earn-to-give' was its showcase example
choices: Sam Bankman-Fried was a prominent EA donor whose 'earn-to-give' was its showcase example
FTX itself had been built by the Center for Effective Altruism's engineering team
EA leaders had publicly opposed Bankman-Fried before his crimes were discovered
FTX users were almost entirely identified as members of EA Forum participants
context: EA had positioned 'earning to give' as a serious moral career — make money, donate to high-impact causes. Bankman-Fried became its highest-profile example. After FTX collapsed in November 2022 and the fraud became clear, EA was forced to reckon with how much it had vouched for him.

question: Stable Diffusion — one of the most influential open-weights image-generation models — was released in:
answer: August 2022, by Stability AI and collaborators
choices: August 2022, by Stability AI and collaborators
January 2023, by Midjourney and collaborators
March 2021, by OpenAI as part of DALL-E
November 2024, by Stability AI alone
context: Stable Diffusion's release made high-quality text-to-image generation a community technology — runnable on consumer GPUs, freely fine-tunable. The democratization changed the field; the deepfake and image-manipulation risks scaled with it. A genuinely open-weights moment.

question: AlphaFold's 2024 Nobel-winning predicted-structure database currently covers approximately:
answer: Over 200 million proteins from a million species
choices: Over 200 million proteins from a million species
Approximately 200 thousand proteins, only from humans
About 5 million proteins, mostly from model organisms
Effectively all life — the dataset is exhaustive and complete
context: DeepMind and EMBL-EBI released the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database in 2022, expanding it from about 1M structures to 200M+ — a 200× jump. Freely available; over 2 million researchers in 190 countries have used it. A real win for AI in basic science.

question: The first publicly visible AI-generated viral hoax of the post-ChatGPT era featured Pope Francis in:
answer: A puffy white designer jacket — an AI-generated image that fooled millions in March 2023
choices: A puffy white designer jacket — an AI-generated image that fooled millions in March 2023
A military uniform, doctored by traditional Photoshop tools in 2022
A Russian Orthodox bishop's robe at the start of the war in Ukraine
A photoshopped wedding photo from a deepfake video site in 2024
context: March 2023: a Midjourney-generated image of Pope Francis in a stylish white jacket spread across social media. Many people, including journalists, believed it real. A small early case study in how AI imagery would interact with viral platforms — and how fast 'a photo on social media' lost its automatic credibility.

question: ImageNet — the dataset whose 2012 competition launched the deep-learning era — was assembled by:
answer: Fei-Fei Li and collaborators at Princeton and Stanford
choices: Fei-Fei Li and collaborators at Princeton and Stanford
Geoffrey Hinton and his team at Google
Yann LeCun and his team at Bell Labs
Demis Hassabis and his team at DeepMind
context: Fei-Fei Li, then at Princeton, launched ImageNet in 2009 — a massive labeled image dataset, built partly via Amazon Mechanical Turk. Without ImageNet, AlexNet would have had nothing to train on. Data infrastructure is half the deep-learning story; it just gets less press than the models.

question: GitHub Copilot — the first widely-used AI coding assistant — was released by GitHub and OpenAI in:
answer: 2021, becoming generally available the next year
choices: 2021, becoming generally available the next year
2019, alongside the release of GPT-2 by OpenAI
2023, after the release of GPT-4 to developers
2024, alongside the release of Copilot for Microsoft Word
context: GitHub Copilot launched in June 2021, built on OpenAI's Codex (a GPT descendant fine-tuned on code). The product launched the AI-coding-assistant category — Cursor, Cody, Codeium, Tabnine, and others followed. Code generation became one of the first commercially proven LLM applications.

question: ImageNet's 2012 success drove AI researchers toward a hardware platform that until then had been mostly a gaming tool. The platform was:
answer: NVIDIA's general-purpose GPU computing, made accessible by CUDA
choices: NVIDIA's general-purpose GPU computing, made accessible by CUDA
Intel's Xeon Phi accelerator, never widely adopted beyond HPC labs
Apple's first ARM-based laptops, popular for client-side AI work
Google's TPU chips, which were not in fact released until 2016
context: NVIDIA's CUDA platform — released 2007 — let researchers program GPUs for general math. AlexNet trained on two consumer GPUs. By 2015, NVIDIA pivoted toward AI as a market; by 2024, it was the most valuable chip company in the world. Hardware choices shape what research becomes possible.

question: DeepMind's AlphaFold predicts:
answer: The 3D structure of a protein from its amino-acid sequence
choices: The 3D structure of a protein from its amino-acid sequence
The function of a gene based on its DNA sequence alone
The boiling point of a chemical based on its molecular formula
The reactivity of an enzyme based on its evolutionary history
context: Proteins are strings of amino acids that fold into shapes; shape determines function. AlphaFold takes the sequence and predicts the fold to near-experimental accuracy. Decades of expensive X-ray crystallography work now have a fast AI complement. A real, useful AI win in basic science.

question: Google Translate moved to neural networks in 2016, replacing its older phrase-based system. The result for most major language pairs:
answer: A noticeable jump in fluency, with the new system reading more like human translation
choices: A noticeable jump in fluency, with the new system reading more like human translation
Almost no perceptible change — users could not tell the difference
Worse output — neural systems were noisier than the older statistical methods
A modest improvement only in English; other pairs saw no real change at all
context: Google Neural Machine Translation, deployed 2016, was a watershed. Bilingual users could feel the difference. Modern LLMs now handle translation as a side effect — the quality on the major languages is near-human; on low-resource languages, gaps remain real.

question: YouTube's recommendation algorithm is optimized primarily to maximize:
answer: Watch time and engagement — not the user's broader wellbeing or accuracy
choices: Watch time and engagement — not the user's broader wellbeing or accuracy
The factual accuracy of every recommended video, on independent fact-check
The political balance of the user's media diet for civic health
The user's stated preferences as explicitly set in their account settings
context: Recommendation systems optimize what their owners measure. YouTube measures watch time; TikTok measures engagement. The objective shapes what surfaces. Knowing what an algorithm is paid to do is essential to understanding why it shows you what it shows you.

question: Netflix and Spotify recommendations are driven by AI that mainly uses:
answer: Collaborative filtering — finding patterns across what similar users have watched or heard
choices: Collaborative filtering — finding patterns across what similar users have watched or heard
Generative AI — making up new movies and songs for each viewer
Mind reading — reading user thoughts through phone microphone signals
Random selection — every recommendation is independent of past use
context: Collaborative filtering: 'people who liked X also liked Y' generalized at huge scale. It dominated recommendation for two decades. Newer hybrid systems mix it with deep-learning embeddings of items themselves. The math is old; the operational scale is what is new.

question: An AI-generated 'deepfake' video typically:
answer: Swaps one person's face onto another's body in a real video
choices: Swaps one person's face onto another's body in a real video
Generates an entirely new video frame by frame from scratch text only
Edits a video's metadata to misrepresent its origin or date alone
Adds AI-generated subtitles to disguise the speaker's true language
context: Classic deepfakes face-swap a target onto existing video. Newer text-to-video models (Sora, Veo) generate from scratch. Detection is an arms race; the practical advice for ordinary people is to verify out-of-band — call back, ask the safe word — when the stakes are high.

question: Modern image-generation models like Midjourney and Stable Diffusion are 'diffusion models.' They start from:
answer: Pure noise, gradually denoised into an image guided by the text prompt
choices: Pure noise, gradually denoised into an image guided by the text prompt
A nearly-final image, slightly edited to match the prompt at the end
A real photograph from the training set, then heavily modified to fit
A wireframe sketch generated by a separate model, then colored in
context: Diffusion models learn to undo the gradual corruption of training images by noise. At generation time, they invert the process — starting from random noise, denoising step by step. The prompt steers the denoising. Each output is structurally fresh; not a collage of training images.

question: DeepMind's AlphaGo's victory cost the human champion a significant share of his earnings — but it also led him to a notable later decision:
answer: Lee Sedol retired from professional Go in 2019, citing the AI's emergence
choices: Lee Sedol retired from professional Go in 2019, citing the AI's emergence
Lee Sedol joined DeepMind as a research advisor on game-playing AI
Lee Sedol founded a Go-themed cryptocurrency exchange in Seoul
Lee Sedol filed a lawsuit against DeepMind for tournament damages
context: Lee Sedol retired from professional Go in 2019. He said the rise of AI had taken something from the meaning of mastery — he could improve, but a machine would always be ahead. A serious answer that gets less coverage than triumphalist 'AI beats human' headlines.

question: Companies using AI to screen job applicants — services like HireVue or Pymetrics — typically:
answer: Score video interviews, gamified assessments, or resumes by trained models
choices: Score video interviews, gamified assessments, or resumes by trained models
Have a live AI hold the entire job interview by voice with no human present
Read the candidate's personal social-media data for the entire prior decade
Use brain scans to read the candidate's thoughts during the interview
context: Algorithmic hiring screens at scale. The bias-and-validity questions are real — what is the model really measuring, and on whose data was it trained? Critics include the EEOC and civil-rights groups. Several state laws (Illinois, NYC) now require disclosure and audit.

question: AI tools used by school administrators to monitor student communications — Gaggle, GoGuardian, Bark — typically:
answer: Scan emails, documents, and chat for keywords flagged by school policy
choices: Scan emails, documents, and chat for keywords flagged by school policy
Listen through every classroom's microphones during the school day
Read students' handwritten notes via tiny webcams in every classroom
Track every student's location via GPS at all times of day
context: School-monitoring AI scans cloud-based student communications for self-harm, threats, and policy violations. The intent — catching kids in crisis — is real; the surveillance footprint is also real. Parents often discover the systems exist only after a flag triggers an administrative action.

question: Most household 'smart speakers' — Alexa, Google Home — actively process audio:
answer: By keeping a small wake-word detector running locally; full audio is sent only after the wake word
choices: By keeping a small wake-word detector running locally; full audio is sent only after the wake word
By sending all room audio continuously to the cloud at all times
By recording audio to a local SD card that is never connected to the internet
By processing all audio entirely locally, with no cloud connection ever
context: Officially: a wake-word detector runs locally, and audio leaves the device only after activation. In practice: false activations happen, and 'accidentally collected' audio has been retained for review by contractors. The system can be designed well; the implementation by big platforms has had public failures.

question: TikTok's recommendation algorithm — widely considered uniquely effective at engagement — is also notable for:
answer: Being controlled by ByteDance, a Chinese company subject to Chinese data law
choices: Being controlled by ByteDance, a Chinese company subject to Chinese data law
Being open-source and auditable by any independent researcher freely
Being entirely controlled by an EU-based subsidiary in Dublin, Ireland
Being legally identical in every respect to YouTube's recommendation system
context: TikTok's parent ByteDance is headquartered in Beijing. Chinese data law lets the state compel cooperation from domestic firms. The US has cited this in attempts to ban or force divestment of TikTok. The recommendation algorithm itself is highly engaging — whatever you think of the geopolitics.

question: An AI chatbot used as a customer-service agent typically:
answer: Handles common requests cheaply, escalating harder ones to a human agent
choices: Handles common requests cheaply, escalating harder ones to a human agent
Replaces all human agents entirely in every customer-service tier
Is run only at very large enterprises with internal AI teams
Is required by federal law to identify itself as AI on every call
context: Customer-service is one of the biggest near-term AI applications. The economics are clear: cheap chatbot for the easy 80% of tickets, human for the hard 20%. Some jurisdictions (California, EU) require disclosure that the user is talking to AI. Most do not — yet.

question: AI-driven dating apps optimize their matching algorithms primarily to:
answer: Keep users engaged with the app — not strictly to find lasting relationships
choices: Keep users engaged with the app — not strictly to find lasting relationships
Maximize the number of marriages produced by their users yearly
Match people who are most likely to become parents within five years
Pair users with the highest-scoring compatibility on a single fixed metric
context: Dating apps make money when users stay on the app. A perfectly successful matching algorithm — one couple per user — would kill the business model. The incentive misalignment is structural. Users sometimes report finding partners despite the app, not because of it.

question: Cybersecurity AI is generally used to:
answer: Detect anomalous traffic and behavior that may indicate an intrusion
choices: Detect anomalous traffic and behavior that may indicate an intrusion
Generate computer viruses that are immune to antivirus detection
Read encrypted communications without needing the decryption key
Physically secure server rooms against unauthorized human entry
context: Anomaly-detection ML is a workhorse of corporate cybersecurity. The model learns 'normal' traffic and behavior, then flags deviations. False positives are noisy but manageable; missed attacks are the real cost. Modern AI is on both sides of the cyber battlefield — defense and offense.

question: AI used by an employer to monitor employee productivity — Microsoft Viva, Hubstaff, etc. — usually:
answer: Tracks keystrokes, mouse activity, app usage, and email/chat patterns
choices: Tracks keystrokes, mouse activity, app usage, and email/chat patterns
Reads the employee's medical records for productivity disorders only
Records every word the employee speaks at home as well as at work
Uses brain-scan technology to track every employee's focus daily
context: Employee-surveillance tools became standard around remote work in 2020-2021. They measure activity proxies — clicks, typing, time in apps — not productivity directly. The proxies can mismeasure deep work (less typing) and reward performative busyness. Workers often discover them only after they are deployed.

question: Families are increasingly advised to set up a 'safe word' shared across the household. The point of the safe word is:
answer: An AI voice clone cannot know it, even if it perfectly mimics the speaker
choices: An AI voice clone cannot know it, even if it perfectly mimics the speaker
A polite signal that the caller does not want to discuss family matters
A password for the family's online banking, shared by all members
A code that automatically blocks the caller's number from future calls
context: AI can clone a voice; it cannot clone family knowledge. A safe word — agreed in advance, never shared by text, asked for in any emergency call — is a cheap, reliable test. Add one for kids, parents, grandparents. Two minutes of preparation; one phone call saved.

question: A friend's social media account starts sending strange messages asking for money or login codes. The most likely explanation is:
answer: The account has been hacked or impersonated — verify out of band before responding
choices: The account has been hacked or impersonated — verify out of band before responding
Your friend is in real urgent trouble — send what they ask immediately
Your friend is testing your loyalty in a friendship game on the platform
The platform has automatically generated the message on the friend's behalf
context: Social-media account takeovers and impersonations are routine. The scammer is counting on familiar names and urgency to bypass thinking. Always verify via a separate channel — phone call, in-person, different app. The friend in trouble can wait one more minute for you to check.

question: A video appears showing a politician saying something shocking. Before sharing, the right step is to:
answer: Check whether reputable sources have reported the same statement independently
choices: Check whether reputable sources have reported the same statement independently
Share quickly — important information should travel fast on social media
Trust if the video has high resolution and clear audio in the moment
Trust if the video is shared by someone with a verified account
context: Deepfake video of public figures has been viable for years and is now cheap. A clip alone is not evidence. Triangulation across reputable sources — and a search for context — is the basic discipline. The cost of a five-minute check is far smaller than the cost of being part of a viral falsehood.

question: A chatbot is asked to write an essay and produces a confident citation to 'Smith and Wong (2017), Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience.' Before using the citation, the wise step is:
answer: Search for the paper online — many AI citations are entirely fabricated
choices: Search for the paper online — many AI citations are entirely fabricated
Trust the citation because it is specific and looks like a real journal
Cite the source secondhand by saying 'cited in ChatGPT' in your essay
Trust the citation if it appears in the model's first response only
context: The Mata v. Avianca case (2023) became famous because a lawyer cited six fake ChatGPT-generated cases in a brief and was fined. Citations are a classic hallucination zone. The model has learned what citations look like, not what is true. Always verify — it takes seconds.

question: A 'phishing' attack — increasingly AI-assisted — typically tries to:
answer: Trick you into entering your password on a fake site that looks real
choices: Trick you into entering your password on a fake site that looks real
Steal data from your computer by exploiting a network vulnerability directly
Crash the website you are trying to visit by flooding it with traffic
Convince you to physically mail your credit card to a foreign address
context: AI lets attackers write fluent, personalized phishing in any language. The defense has not changed: never enter credentials from a link in an email. Type the URL yourself or use a bookmark. Hover over links before clicking. Slow down when the message tells you to hurry.

question: Among popular messaging apps, the strongest end-to-end encryption and minimal-metadata design is found in:
answer: Signal
choices: Signal
Facebook Messenger
Telegram
WeChat
context: Signal is end-to-end encrypted by default, open source, and minimizes metadata it collects. WhatsApp uses the same encryption protocol but is owned by Meta and collects metadata. Telegram is encrypted only in 'secret chats'; WeChat is monitored extensively by Chinese authorities. Worth knowing the difference.

question: Privacy-focused alternatives to Gmail, Google Drive, and Google's VPN are offered by Swiss-based:
answer: Proton — Mail, Drive, VPN, and a calendar with end-to-end encryption
choices: Proton — Mail, Drive, VPN, and a calendar with end-to-end encryption
Tutanota — only an email provider, not a full suite of tools
DuckDuckGo — only a search engine, not an email or storage provider
Mojeek — only a search engine, not an email or storage provider
context: Proton started as ProtonMail and expanded into Drive, VPN, Calendar, and a password manager. End-to-end encryption is the default; the company runs out of Switzerland under strict privacy law. Not perfect, but the most complete mainstream privacy-first stack as of mid-2020s.

question: An apartment lease or job application asks for permission to use AI-driven 'background check.' The thoughtful step is to:
answer: Ask what data sources will be used and whether you can review the result
choices: Ask what data sources will be used and whether you can review the result
Sign without reading — these forms are required by federal law anyway
Refuse outright — AI in background checks is always illegal in the US
Sign only if it is a long-form lease rather than a job application
context: Under the FCRA, you have the right to know what consumer-reporting agency was used, see the report, and dispute errors. Algorithmic background-check tools have produced wrongful rejections; reading carefully and asking questions is your protection. Defaults are not in your favor.

question: A consumer DNA testing service (23andMe, Ancestry) collecting saliva samples:
answer: Builds a large genetic database that may be sold, breached, or used by police
choices: Builds a large genetic database that may be sold, breached, or used by police
Is required by federal law to destroy samples within thirty days of testing
Operates under HIPAA medical privacy law, fully protecting the data
Encrypts the genetic data so thoroughly that even the company cannot read it
context: 23andMe had a major data breach in 2023 (nearly 7 million users affected). Both 23andMe and Ancestry have shared data with pharmaceutical partners; police have used family-genealogy databases (GEDmatch in particular) to identify suspects via relatives. Your DNA is also your relatives' DNA.

question: Investment 'opportunities' pitched through chat, especially crypto or stock-tip groups, increasingly use AI to:
answer: Generate convincing personas, 'success' screenshots, and consistent backstories
choices: Generate convincing personas, 'success' screenshots, and consistent backstories
Predict the stock market accurately enough to safely promise high returns
Trade legitimately on behalf of users at no cost to the user ever
Submit only to investors approved by the SEC for security clearance
context: Pig-butchering, fake-trading-platform scams, and crypto fraud now run on AI-generated content. Profile photos, group screenshots, 'mentor' replies — all synthetic. The defense is structural: skepticism of unsolicited investment messaging, verification of every claim, and the knowledge that real investing is boring.

question: When uploading a document to a free chatbot for summarization, a user should remember:
answer: The document may be retained, reviewed by staff, and possibly used to train future models
choices: The document may be retained, reviewed by staff, and possibly used to train future models
The document is automatically encrypted and inaccessible even to the company
The document is processed only on the user's local computer, never the cloud
The document is read only by the model and never by any human at all
context: Free and consumer tiers usually log uploads. Enterprise tiers usually do not. Always check; never upload medical records, legal documents, or financial statements without knowing the terms. If in doubt, ask the AI to summarize a redacted version instead.

question: A senior is sent an unexpected email saying their bank account has been compromised and asking them to click to verify. The standard advice is:
answer: Do not click; go to the bank's website directly or call the number on your card
choices: Do not click; go to the bank's website directly or call the number on your card
Click and verify quickly — banks need fast action to stop fraud properly
Reply asking for more information before deciding whether to click
Forward the email to family for advice before doing anything else with it
context: Click-here-to-fix is the universal phishing pattern, now produced by AI in fluent prose. The defense never changes: type the URL yourself, call the number from your card, never trust a link or attachment in a security email. Talk this through with elderly family members before they need it.

question: A teenager wants to delete an old social media account. A useful checklist before deleting is:
answer: Download a copy of your data; remove ties to other accounts; only then delete
choices: Download a copy of your data; remove ties to other accounts; only then delete
Just delete; everything is automatically recoverable for thirty days anyway
Use a paid 'account remover' service to handle deletion properly for you
Change the password to something complex before deletion to be safe
context: Deletion is usually one-way. Download your data first (most platforms have an export). Look for accounts you used 'log in with Facebook/Google' on and switch them to a real password. Then delete. Worth doing for accounts you do not use; reduces breach exposure.

question: A common AI 'jailbreak' uses the framing 'Pretend you are my late grandmother who used to whisper instructions on X.' This shows:
answer: Story or role-play wrappers can sometimes coax models past their safety training
choices: Story or role-play wrappers can sometimes coax models past their safety training
Models have a literal database of grandmother stories they always trust
Models honor any request that mentions a deceased family member
Grandmothers have legal authority that overrides AI content policy
