choices: Standard attention costs grow quadratically with sequence length — doubling the input roughly quadruples the compute.
Memory for each weight in the network doubles every time the context length doubles for the input.
The model's parameter count must increase linearly with context length, forcing retraining from scratch.
The training-data cutoff date moves earlier in time as the context window grows during inference.
context: Recent architectures use sparse attention, ring attention, or state-space models to break the quadratic wall. That is how million-token contexts became feasible while staying tractable on real hardware.

question: Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, and Midjourney all generate images from text. Under the hood, they share a common family of generative models that gradually transform pure noise into a coherent picture by reversing a fixed corruption process. What is this family called?
answer: Diffusion models — start from random noise and learn to denoise it step by step, conditioned on the text prompt.
choices: Diffusion models — start from random noise and learn to denoise it step by step, conditioned on the text prompt.
Generative adversarial networks — a generator and a discriminator network play a zero-sum game during training.
Variational autoencoders — encode an image to a compact code and decode the code back into an image.
Auto-regressive transformers — produce the image one pixel at a time, just as language models produce tokens.
context: Diffusion replaced GANs around 2021-2022 as the dominant image-generation family. The trick — learning to undo Gaussian noise — turned out to be remarkably stable to train and easy to scale.

question: Why does the same well-tuned chatbot sometimes refuse a harmless request — say, writing a short villain monologue for a school play — and sometimes happily comply? The most accurate description of why such refusals are inconsistent.
answer: Safety training is statistical, not rule-based; the model has learned a soft pattern of what to refuse, with noisy edges.
choices: Safety training is statistical, not rule-based; the model has learned a soft pattern of what to refuse, with noisy edges.
The chatbot has a separate hand-written rulebook checked before each response, and the rulebook is updated hourly.
Engineers have manually classified every possible request as allowed or refused; mistakes are rare and traceable.
Refusals depend on a hidden score assigned to each user account based on previous interactions with the system.
context: Because the refusal behaviour is learned, it can be inconsistent in ways the developers do not control. That is also why 'safety filters' are filters: they catch most cases, miss some, and over-refuse others — an ongoing trade-off.

question: A method named retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a chatbot answer questions about up-to-the-minute documents without retraining. What does RAG actually do at query time?
answer: Search a document index for snippets relevant to the user's question, then paste those snippets into the model's prompt before generating.
choices: Search a document index for snippets relevant to the user's question, then paste those snippets into the model's prompt before generating.
Update the model's weights from the latest documents the moment the user submits a question to the chatbot.
Distill the document index into a smaller model that is then trained from scratch for every individual question.
Compress the user's question into a vector and compare it directly to vectors stored in the model's weights.
context: RAG is how a customer-support bot can answer using your specific manual, or a legal assistant can quote real cases. The model never 'memorises' the documents — they ride into the prompt at query time.

question: Modern frontier models are evaluated on standardised tests called 'benchmarks' — MMLU for general knowledge, GSM8K for grade-school maths, HumanEval for coding. Why is reading-too-much-into a single benchmark score a known mistake?
answer: Benchmarks leak into training data, get gamed by overfitting, and may not reflect the tasks users actually care about.
choices: Benchmarks leak into training data, get gamed by overfitting, and may not reflect the tasks users actually care about.
Benchmarks are physically run on different hardware, and the same model gives wildly different scores across machines.
Benchmarks are only translated into English, so non-English models always score lower than their actual capabilities warrant.
Benchmarks are kept secret by their authors, so model-makers cannot tell which test their system is being graded on.
context: When test questions appear in pre-training data, models 'remember' them rather than reasoning fresh. New benchmarks get contaminated within months. Treat any single number with skepticism; track many, and ask 'does this match what users see?'

question: Two related but distinct kinds of fine-tuning are used to make a chatbot helpful. The first uses examples of ideal responses; the second uses comparison data — 'response A is better than response B'. What are these two stages usually called?
answer: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on demonstrations, then preference optimisation (e.g. RLHF or DPO) on comparisons.
choices: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on demonstrations, then preference optimisation (e.g. RLHF or DPO) on comparisons.
Pre-training on internet text, then post-training on synthetic data generated by a smaller model in the same family.
Quantization on weights, then distillation on outputs — both done after the base model is fully trained from scratch.
Tokenization on inputs, then embedding on tokens — both happen before training and not as separate training stages.
context: SFT teaches the model what good answers look like. Preference optimisation teaches it to choose better answers between candidates. Both are cheap compared to pre-training, and together they explain the polite assistant feel.

question: Different LLM providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta — use different tokenizers. A sentence costs different numbers of tokens with each. What practical consequence does this have for someone who calls multiple APIs?
answer: Comparing per-token prices across providers is misleading; the same task can cost very different totals depending on tokenizer.
choices: Comparing per-token prices across providers is misleading; the same task can cost very different totals depending on tokenizer.
Switching providers requires retraining your application from scratch, since the tokenizers are mathematically incompatible.
All providers are forced by a 2023 treaty to publish a master tokenizer comparison chart updated monthly.
The choice of tokenizer determines whether the model can speak languages other than English at all.
context: Always benchmark cost in your own use case rather than relying on per-token pricing. A 30 percent cheaper token can still mean a 20 percent more expensive query if the tokenizer splits text more aggressively.

question: What is the practical difference between a 'base model' and an 'instruct' or 'chat' model from the same family — say, Llama 3 base versus Llama 3 Instruct?
answer: Base completes raw text without expecting a conversation; instruct/chat has been fine-tuned to follow instructions in the format users expect.
choices: Base completes raw text without expecting a conversation; instruct/chat has been fine-tuned to follow instructions in the format users expect.
Base runs only on CPUs while instruct runs only on GPUs, due to differences in their underlying architecture.
Base contains all the training data while instruct has been distilled into a smaller form with reduced knowledge.
Base is licensed for research only while instruct is licensed for commercial use under the same family terms.
context: Base models continue your text. Hand one 'What is the capital of France?' and it might write more questions, not the answer. Instruct models have been taught to read that as a request and reply 'Paris'.

question: Two phrases sometimes used loosely turn out to mean different things: 'memorising training data' versus 'learning from training data'. What is the boundary that matters?
answer: A model that can reproduce long passages verbatim has memorised; one that can generalise to new examples has learned patterns — both can co-exist.
choices: A model that can reproduce long passages verbatim has memorised; one that can generalise to new examples has learned patterns — both can co-exist.
Memorising is illegal in the United States while learning is allowed; the boundary is set by federal regulation.
Memorising happens only in the embedding layer while learning happens in the rest of the network's weights.
Memorising occurs during inference; learning occurs only during training and stops once the model is deployed.
context: Verbatim reproduction matters for copyright debates and privacy leaks. Generalisation is what makes models useful. Real models do some of each, and 'how much' depends on data and training choices.

question: Why does a chatbot sometimes claim a recent event happened when it did not — for example, inventing the result of a sports match that has not been played?
answer: Without a search tool, the model has no way to know the current date or recent events, so it confabulates plausible-sounding answers from old patterns.
choices: Without a search tool, the model has no way to know the current date or recent events, so it confabulates plausible-sounding answers from old patterns.
The model has been deliberately programmed to test user fact-checking habits by introducing false claims at random.
The model's internal clock has drifted, causing it to confuse the calendar by exactly one year per response.
The model picks up live signals from the user's webcam and microphone to generate a recent-sounding answer.
context: When asked about events past its training cutoff, a well-designed chatbot says 'I don't know' or uses a search tool. A poorly designed one fluently invents. Always check claimed dates and current events against an external source.

question: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google charge for API calls 'per million tokens', usually with different prices for input versus output. Why is output usually more expensive than input?
answer: Output tokens require running the full network for each new token; input tokens can be processed largely in parallel during the prefill phase.
choices: Output tokens require running the full network for each new token; input tokens can be processed largely in parallel during the prefill phase.
Output tokens require human review before being returned, while input tokens are processed without any human in the loop.
Output tokens are charged at higher rates to discourage long replies and reduce server load on the provider.
Output tokens include hidden formatting characters that take more storage on the provider's servers.
context: This pricing also incentivises shorter responses. Watch the numbers when you do back-of-envelope cost estimates for an LLM app — the output multiplier can dominate cheap-sounding rates.

question: Modern LLMs can use 'tools' — they output a structured request like 'search(query)' or 'calculator(expression)', a wrapper runs it, and the result feeds back into the conversation. What capability does this combine?
answer: The model's pattern-matching language ability with the precision of code, search engines, and databases — each handling what it does best.
choices: The model's pattern-matching language ability with the precision of code, search engines, and databases — each handling what it does best.
The model's training data with a search engine's training data, doubling the total knowledge available to the model.
The model's weights with a calculator's weights, producing a hybrid model that needs no external tools to run.
The model's tokenization with the calculator's tokenization, ensuring both systems use the same vocabulary.
context: Tool-using LLMs are why modern chatbots can do arithmetic, browse the web, run code, and query databases. The trick: format the call, run it externally, feed the result back. Without tools, the LLM is stuck with its training data and no maths.

question: When a model uses a tool to run code, what is the typical security boundary that protects the user's main system from a malicious model action?
answer: Sandboxing — the code runs in an isolated environment with restricted file system, network, and process access.
choices: Sandboxing — the code runs in an isolated environment with restricted file system, network, and process access.
Encryption — the code is encrypted before execution so the user's data cannot be read by the tool.
Compression — the code is compressed before being run so it occupies less memory on the host system.
Translation — the code is translated to a different programming language before being executed in the tool.
context: Sandboxes are not bulletproof but they raise the cost of exploitation considerably. The combination of restricted tools plus careful permissioning is the defensive posture for tool-using AI agents in production.

question: Bigger is not always better: a 70-billion-parameter model fine-tuned for medical use can beat a 700-billion-parameter generalist on medical questions. What general lesson does this illustrate?
answer: Specialised fine-tuning on relevant data can outweigh the raw capacity advantage of a much larger generalist model.
choices: Specialised fine-tuning on relevant data can outweigh the raw capacity advantage of a much larger generalist model.
Medical questions are inherently easier than general questions, so any model trained on medicine wins automatically.
Smaller models always beat larger ones, because their training is more recent and uses better algorithms by default.
Larger models are deliberately handicapped on medical questions to encourage purchase of specialist subscriptions.
context: Smaller, targeted models also run faster and cheaper. For narrow business uses, a fine-tuned 8B-parameter model on your own machines often beats paying a generalist API for everything.

question: What is the practical reason a model performs better when given examples in the prompt — 'few-shot' — than when asked cold?
answer: Examples set the format, style, and reasoning pattern the model should follow, by making them part of the visible context.
choices: Examples set the format, style, and reasoning pattern the model should follow, by making them part of the visible context.
Examples retrain the model's weights mid-conversation, permanently improving its abilities on similar tasks.
Examples disable the model's safety filters, allowing it to give more complete answers without restriction.
Examples encrypt the prompt so other users on the same server cannot read what was asked.
context: Few-shot was the surprise that GPT-3 in 2020 made vivid: feed in two or three examples of what you want, and the model imitates the pattern. No retraining required.

question: Some models are trained with a feature called 'constitutional AI' (Anthropic's approach) where a written constitution guides revision of responses. What is the practical difference from RLHF?
answer: Revisions are driven by AI feedback against written principles, reducing reliance on large numbers of human raters.
choices: Revisions are driven by AI feedback against written principles, reducing reliance on large numbers of human raters.
Revisions happen entirely in the user's web browser, so no model output ever reaches the company's servers.
Revisions are produced by combining outputs from many different models hosted by competing providers.
Revisions only apply to political topics; everything else is handled by ordinary supervised fine-tuning.
context: Constitutional AI scales cheaper than collecting tens of thousands of human preference comparisons. It also makes the values more legible — the constitution can be read and critiqued — though the model can still misinterpret it in practice.

question: What does the abbreviation 'AGI' commonly stand for, and why is it controversial to define?
answer: Artificial General Intelligence — capable of human-level performance across most cognitive tasks; the threshold for 'most' is undefined.
choices: Artificial General Intelligence — capable of human-level performance across most cognitive tasks; the threshold for 'most' is undefined.
Algorithmic Genetic Inference — a particular method of training models using simulated evolution.
Automated Graphics Interpretation — a class of computer vision systems for industrial image processing.
Active Gradient Iteration — a variant of gradient descent used to train very deep networks.
context: The goalposts move: tasks once thought to require AGI (chess, Go, fluent translation) keep falling to specialised systems. 'AGI in 5 years' has been predicted for sixty years. Treat any confident timeline with appropriate skepticism.

question: Why is 'pre-training' described as 'self-supervised' even though it produces a model that responds to questions?
answer: The labels come from the text itself: predict the next token given the previous ones. No human labeling is required.
choices: The labels come from the text itself: predict the next token given the previous ones. No human labeling is required.
Engineers add labels to every sentence in the training corpus by hand, then train the model in a supervised loop.
The model labels its own outputs at inference time and uses those labels to update weights on the fly.
The training corpus is fully unlabeled and the model learns purely by clustering similar sentences together.
context: Self-supervised learning was the unlock for scale: the entire internet becomes free training data because the labels are extracted from the text itself. This is why pre-training on trillions of tokens became feasible.

question: Why might two different models — say, ChatGPT and Claude — produce noticeably different tones from the same prompt, even when their underlying technology is similar?
answer: Different RLHF data, different fine-tuning choices, and different system prompts shape distinct response personalities.
choices: Different RLHF data, different fine-tuning choices, and different system prompts shape distinct response personalities.
Different chip manufacturers produce different audio outputs, which propagate to the model's text behaviour.
Different time zones in which the providers are headquartered cause subtle shifts in word choice.
Different page colours on the chat website cause the model to use different word choices.
context: Personality is engineered. Engineers pick examples and raters, write constitutions or guidelines, and ship a specific voice. The 'model' is one layer; the assistant on top of it is another product entirely.

question: When training data includes the same web page hundreds of times under different URLs, the model can over-memorise its content. What is the standard mitigation called?
answer: Deduplication — identifying and removing or down-weighting near-duplicate documents before training.
choices: Deduplication — identifying and removing or down-weighting near-duplicate documents before training.
Tokenization — splitting text into subword pieces so each piece is rare enough to avoid memorisation.
Quantization — reducing the precision of weights to make exact memorisation mathematically impossible.
Attention dropout — randomly removing attention weights during training so memorisation gets washed out.
context: Common Crawl alone contains many near-copies of the same text. Careful deduplication is one of the unglamorous data-engineering jobs that quietly determines how good a frontier model ends up being.

question: A model returns a numerical 'confidence' or log probability for each token. Is this number a reliable indicator of factual correctness?
answer: No — high token-level confidence often coincides with confident wrong answers, especially for facts not in training.
choices: No — high token-level confidence often coincides with confident wrong answers, especially for facts not in training.
Yes — every modern model is calibrated so 90% confidence means 90% correct over many calls.
Yes — confidence is a separate channel computed by a smaller fact-checking model running in parallel.
Yes — the chip manufacturer's standard guarantees confidence accuracy within one percent.
context: Calibration research is active and partial. The most honest summary: a confident-sounding answer is not evidence of correctness; verify factual claims against an external source.

question: How does a 'denoising' diffusion model relate to learning to generate images from text?
answer: It learns to remove Gaussian noise step by step, conditioned on a text prompt, until clean image content emerges.
choices: It learns to remove Gaussian noise step by step, conditioned on a text prompt, until clean image content emerges.
It compresses an image to a smaller version, then trains a separate model to enlarge it back to the original size.
It searches a database of training images for the closest match to the text prompt and returns that image.
It generates a single random image and then asks the user to rate it, iterating until the user is satisfied.
context: The 'reverse diffusion' trick — learning to undo Gaussian noise — turned out to be remarkably stable to train. It is the backbone of Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 3, and Midjourney.

question: Why is it standard practice to evaluate a trained model on a 'held-out' test set the model never saw during training?
answer: Performance on the training data is an optimistic measure; held-out data tests whether the model generalises.
choices: Performance on the training data is an optimistic measure; held-out data tests whether the model generalises.
Training data is encrypted after training, so it cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.
Test data is more recent than training data, which is always older than the day the model was deployed.
Test data is provided by regulatory agencies to ensure compliance with industry standards.
context: If you tune on the test set, you have effectively trained on it; the test must stay clean. This is the classic discipline that distinguishes real ML practice from cargo-cult benchmark chasing.

question: A 'context distillation' technique trains a student model to imitate not just a teacher's outputs but its internal logits — the probability distribution over next tokens. Why might that produce a better student?
answer: Logits carry richer information than the chosen token alone, including how unsure the teacher was between alternatives.
choices: Logits carry richer information than the chosen token alone, including how unsure the teacher was between alternatives.
Logits are encrypted versions of the weights, so the student inherits the teacher's parameters directly.
Logits include the teacher's training data, transferring it into the student without licensing fees.
Logits are run on specialised hardware that the student inherits along with the trained weights.
context: Distillation from logits — sometimes called 'soft labels' — is part of how big closed models get compressed into smaller open ones. Knowledge that lived in the gradients moves to the smaller student.

question: When a chatbot is asked a question outside its training data — for example, a private internal company process — it cannot recover the answer. What is the standard remedy?
answer: Retrieval-augmented generation: provide the relevant documents in the prompt at query time.
choices: Retrieval-augmented generation: provide the relevant documents in the prompt at query time.
Train an entirely new model on the company's documents, costing tens of millions of dollars per query.
Ask the chatbot more loudly, since the model has a hidden volume parameter that triggers deeper knowledge.
Switch to a different chatbot, since each chatbot is trained on a different company's internal documents.
context: RAG is how enterprise chatbots work in practice. Index your docs, retrieve a few relevant snippets, paste them into the prompt, let the model write the answer. The model is the language layer; the docs are the truth layer.

question: Why are 'reasoning models' (such as OpenAI's o-series) sometimes slower and more expensive per query than ordinary chatbots?
answer: They spend much more compute on internal reasoning steps before producing the final answer.
choices: They spend much more compute on internal reasoning steps before producing the final answer.
They are physically located on slower servers in remote datacenters to ensure higher security.
They are deliberately throttled to keep them at the same price as competing products from other companies.
They run on older chips that are slower than the ones used for ordinary chatbots.
context: These models burn many more tokens internally — sometimes hidden from the user — to reason step by step before answering. Trade-off: higher cost and latency for better performance on hard problems, especially maths and coding.

question: Why does it matter that frontier model training uses billions of dollars of compute concentrated in a few datacenters?
answer: The capital and infrastructure barriers concentrate frontier capabilities among a handful of organisations.
choices: The capital and infrastructure barriers concentrate frontier capabilities among a handful of organisations.
The datacenters generate too much heat for the local environment, forcing models to be small.
The shared infrastructure means every model in the world has identical capabilities.
The cost is offset by sharing weights freely, so concentration has no practical effect on access.
context: Concentration matters for who decides values, refusals, and product priorities. Open-weights models — Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek — are the countervailing force, but they still depend on access to massive training compute.

question: If you wanted to run a frontier-quality LLM on your laptop, with full privacy and no API calls, what is the typical bottleneck on a 2024-era machine?
answer: RAM and GPU memory — frontier models in full precision do not fit; quantized open-source models are the realistic option.
choices: RAM and GPU memory — frontier models in full precision do not fit; quantized open-source models are the realistic option.
Hard disk space — frontier models occupy more storage than the typical laptop hard drive.
Internet bandwidth — local models require constant connection to the model provider's servers.
Battery life — local models drain a laptop in seconds even when plugged in.
context: A 70B model at 4-bit quantization runs on 48GB of GPU RAM. Smaller models (8B-14B) run on consumer hardware. The trade-off is quality versus what fits — and many users are satisfied with the smaller models.

question: In 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published a book called *Perceptrons*. Their analysis showed limits of a particular kind of network and contributed to a downturn in AI research funding. What did they prove about single-layer perceptrons?
answer: They cannot learn certain simple functions — most famously XOR — because such functions are not linearly separable.
choices: They cannot learn certain simple functions — most famously XOR — because such functions are not linearly separable.
They cannot run on the IBM computers available at the time due to insufficient memory capacity for their weights.
They cannot be trained without supervised data, and supervised data was impossible to obtain in any quantity.
They cannot work with images larger than ten pixels by ten pixels, ruling out practical applications.
context: The proof was correct but the conclusion overshot. Multi-layer networks can learn XOR — but training them required backpropagation, which Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams would popularise only in 1986.

question: In 1986, David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams published a paper in Nature that popularised an algorithm later credited as one of the key engines of the deep learning revolution. What algorithm?
answer: Backpropagation — efficient computation of gradients through a multi-layer network via the chain rule of calculus.
choices: Backpropagation — efficient computation of gradients through a multi-layer network via the chain rule of calculus.
Gradient boosting — sequentially training small models that each correct the errors of the previous ones.
Self-organising maps — an unsupervised network that produces low-dimensional projections of high-dimensional data.
Hopfield networks — a fully connected network for storing and recalling fixed patterns by associative memory.
context: Backprop had been independently discovered several times — by Linnainmaa in 1970, by Werbos in 1974 — but the 1986 paper was when the AI community latched on. Hinton later wrote that he thought it would solve everything; in fact it took another 25 years.

question: At Bell Labs in 1989, Yann LeCun built a network to read handwritten digits on cheques. It used a particular architecture that scanned a small filter across the input image. What was this network called, and what architecture did it pioneer?
answer: LeNet — an early convolutional neural network, the design that would later power modern image recognition.
choices: LeNet — an early convolutional neural network, the design that would later power modern image recognition.
DeepNet — a precursor to the deep recurrent networks that handle speech recognition today.
AlexNet — an early version of the network that won ImageNet, deployed at Bell Labs years before the 2012 paper.
MicroNet — a small dense network used to classify postal codes on US mail at the time.
context: LeNet read US Postal Service mail and bank cheques for years. The convolutional design — local filters, weight sharing, pooling — was rediscovered and scaled up by AlexNet two decades later for the ImageNet revolution.

question: In 2012, three University of Toronto researchers — Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton — entered the ImageNet image classification competition with a network that crushed the previous best. What was the network called?
answer: AlexNet — a convolutional neural network that cut top-5 error from 26% to 15% and triggered the deep learning revolution.
choices: AlexNet — a convolutional neural network that cut top-5 error from 26% to 15% and triggered the deep learning revolution.
DeepDream — a Google-built visualisation system that produced surreal hallucinatory images from photographs.
GoogLeNet — Google's deeper network that won ImageNet two years later with the famous 'inception' module.
VGGNet — Oxford's simpler but very deep network that was a leading entry in the 2014 ImageNet competition.
context: AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GTX 580 graphics cards in Krizhevsky's bedroom at his parents' house. The win — by a huge margin, with deep learning trouncing hand-crafted features — was the moment the field changed.

question: In June 2017, eight researchers at Google Brain published a paper titled 'Attention Is All You Need' in NeurIPS. It introduced a new neural network design built around a self-attention mechanism. What name did the paper give the design?
answer: The transformer — a model that processes whole sequences in parallel using stacked self-attention and feed-forward layers.
choices: The transformer — a model that processes whole sequences in parallel using stacked self-attention and feed-forward layers.
The convolver — a deep stack of convolutional layers with explicit positional encoding built in.
The recurrer — a faster variant of the recurrent neural network with parallelisable training.
The expander — a model that grows in depth during training based on data complexity.
context: Lead author Ashish Vaswani and seven coauthors. The paper became one of the most cited in computer science history. Every modern chatbot — GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama — is descended from this design.

question: In October 2018, Google released a model called BERT, which dominated natural-language benchmarks for the next year. What did BERT do differently from previous transformer-based models?
answer: It read sequences bidirectionally — masking random tokens and predicting them from surrounding context on both sides.
choices: It read sequences bidirectionally — masking random tokens and predicting them from surrounding context on both sides.
It read sequences from right to left, the reverse of GPT, demonstrating better performance on questions.
It used no attention at all — a deeper recurrent network with carefully tuned hyperparameters.
It abandoned the transformer architecture entirely and returned to convolutional sequence models.
context: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) was the encoder-only sibling of GPT's decoder-only family. It powered Google Search ranking for years and was the model students cut their teeth on in NLP courses circa 2019.

question: OpenAI's GPT-3 paper, 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners', was published in May 2020. The model had a parameter count that was an order of magnitude larger than previous published language models. How many parameters?
answer: 175 billion — roughly ten times the size of the largest published model before it, and the model that introduced 'in-context learning' to wide attention.
choices: 175 billion — roughly ten times the size of the largest published model before it, and the model that introduced 'in-context learning' to wide attention.
1.5 billion — the largest GPT-2 version, scaled up tenfold relative to research norms but not by an order of magnitude.
1 trillion — the rumoured size of GPT-4 three years later, often confused with GPT-3 in popular coverage.
17 billion — about twice the size of leading research models of 2020 but not the size announced for GPT-3.
context: GPT-3 was the watershed: 175 billion parameters made few-shot prompting reliably work without task-specific fine-tuning. It quietly powered some products until ChatGPT made the family famous two years later.

question: Demis Hassabis founded DeepMind in 2010, which Google acquired in 2014. In 2020 the lab released a system that solved one of biology's standing grand challenges: predicting how proteins fold from their amino acid sequence. What was the system called?
answer: AlphaFold — by 2024 it had predicted structures for over 200 million proteins, made freely available to researchers worldwide.
choices: AlphaFold — by 2024 it had predicted structures for over 200 million proteins, made freely available to researchers worldwide.
DeepBio — a parallel project at DeepMind focused on cellular biology rather than protein structure.
FoldNet — the original 2018 neural network for protein folding before the AlphaFold name was adopted.
ProtAI — a competing IBM project that achieved similar accuracy in protein folding around the same time.
context: Hassabis and AlphaFold's John Jumper shared half the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The other half went to David Baker. Protein structure went from PhDs of work per protein to a database lookup — a real, scientific transformation.

question: In October 2024, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics to two researchers for foundational work on machine learning with artificial neural networks. Who were they?
answer: John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton — for the Hopfield network and the Boltzmann machine, foundational to modern deep learning.
choices: John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton — for the Hopfield network and the Boltzmann machine, foundational to modern deep learning.
Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio — for convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks respectively.
Ilya Sutskever and Dario Amodei — for the development of GPT and Claude language models.
Demis Hassabis and John Jumper — for AlphaGo and AlphaFold, awarded the same week as their Chemistry prize.
context: Both prizes — Physics for Hopfield and Hinton, Chemistry for Hassabis, Jumper, and Baker — were milestones in AI's emergence as a recognised scientific discipline. Hinton called it 'amazing' that physics had recognised neural networks.

question: Yann LeCun is one of the three 2018 Turing Award winners and currently serves as Meta's Chief AI Scientist. Among prominent AI researchers, he is known for a specific public position on existential AI risk. What is that position?
answer: He is publicly skeptical of doomerism, arguing that the most catastrophic scenarios are speculative and that fears divert attention from real near-term concerns.
choices: He is publicly skeptical of doomerism, arguing that the most catastrophic scenarios are speculative and that fears divert attention from real near-term concerns.
He is the most vocal proponent of AI doomerism, regularly calling for moratoria on training large models.
He has refused to comment publicly on AI risk, considering it outside the scope of his research interests.
He has called for the United Nations to take over all AI development immediately and permanently.
context: LeCun's skepticism — he argues current systems are far from any kind of agency or goal-pursuing — is one of the substantive scientific counterweights to the Yudkowsky-Bostrom apocalyptic framing.

question: Ilya Sutskever co-founded OpenAI in 2015. After the November 2023 board drama, he eventually departed to found a new company in mid-2024 with a deliberately narrow mission. What did he name the new company?
answer: Safe Superintelligence Inc. — a single-product company with the stated goal of building safe superintelligent AI.
choices: Safe Superintelligence Inc. — a single-product company with the stated goal of building safe superintelligent AI.
Open Source AI — a non-profit dedicated to releasing open-weights versions of frontier models.
Computational Alignment Labs — a research lab focused on mathematical formal verification of AI systems.
DeepCognition — a competitor to DeepMind specialising in cognitive science applications of AI.
context: Sutskever's new company raised over a billion dollars without releasing a product. Whether 'safe superintelligence' is engineering achievable, ideologically motivated, or a fundraising posture is a debate the field will continue.

question: On March 28, 2023, the Future of Life Institute published an open letter signed by more than 30,000 people calling for a pause in training models more powerful than GPT-4. Among the signatories was a particularly visible pair of tech figures. Who were they?
answer: Elon Musk and Steve Wozniak — alongside Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell, and Yuval Noah Harari among many others.
choices: Elon Musk and Steve Wozniak — alongside Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell, and Yuval Noah Harari among many others.
Bill Gates and Tim Cook — alongside other tech CEOs from the Bay Area's largest companies.
Mark Zuckerberg and Sundar Pichai — both publicly distancing their companies from the most aggressive frontier work.
Jeff Bezos and Larry Ellison — joined by Oracle and Amazon Web Services chief executives.
context: Musk's signature was particularly noted given his earlier role as OpenAI co-founder. Critics argued the letter favoured incumbents. No major lab honoured the pause. The letter is now a documentary fact of the field's politics in 2023.

question: On October 16, 2023, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen published a 5,200-word essay on the Andreessen Horowitz blog that became the manifesto of a movement called 'effective accelerationism' (e/acc). What was the essay titled?
answer: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto — arguing that technology is an unalloyed good and regulatory restraint is the main obstacle to flourishing.
choices: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto — arguing that technology is an unalloyed good and regulatory restraint is the main obstacle to flourishing.
The Acceleration Imperative — making the case for accelerating AI development to outpace foreign competitors.
Why Software Is Eating the World — Andreessen's earlier essay republished with new commentary.
The Rational Optimist — co-authored with Matt Ridley as a sequel to Ridley's earlier book.
context: E/acc was framed as the symmetrical opposite of EA doomerism. Both camps share a similar disposition — high agency, sweeping moral claims — but reach opposite conclusions. The bank treats both as ideologies.

question: Sam Bankman-Fried's cryptocurrency exchange FTX collapsed in November 2022. SBF was a high-profile figure in a specific philosophical movement that had been funding AI safety research at scale. What was that movement called?
answer: Effective altruism (EA) — the utilitarian charity movement that became deeply entwined with AI safety funding.
choices: Effective altruism (EA) — the utilitarian charity movement that became deeply entwined with AI safety funding.
Stoicism — the ancient Greek school of philosophy that had been adopted by Silicon Valley figures.
Objectivism — Ayn Rand's school of thought that influenced libertarian-leaning tech investors.
Universalism — a recently revived Enlightenment-era humanitarian framework.
context: FTX-linked grants had been flowing into AI safety research, including to MIRI, the Future of Life Institute, and Future of Humanity Institute. SBF was convicted on seven fraud counts in November 2023 and sentenced to 25 years in 2024.

question: In late February 2024, Google paused image generation in its Gemini chatbot after users posted screenshots of historically absurd outputs. Among the most circulated were Nazi soldiers and US Founding Fathers rendered as racially diverse groups. Who issued the apology?
answer: Sundar Pichai, Google's CEO, called the responses 'completely unacceptable' in an internal memo.
choices: Sundar Pichai, Google's CEO, called the responses 'completely unacceptable' in an internal memo.
Sergey Brin, Google's co-founder, returned from retirement to issue a public apology to users.
Demis Hassabis, head of Google DeepMind, refused to apologise and defended the diversity tuning.
An automated company statement was issued without any named executive taking responsibility.
context: Alphabet lost about $96.9 billion in market value over the episode. The bank's frame: this was not an isolated bug but a vivid illustration of how alignment choices encode value commitments — sometimes catastrophically.

question: President Biden signed Executive Order 14110 on AI safety on October 30, 2023. It directed agencies like NIST to develop safety standards and required reporting from labs running very large training jobs. What happened to the order under the next administration?
answer: President Trump rescinded it on January 20, 2025, in one of his first executive actions on taking office.
choices: President Trump rescinded it on January 20, 2025, in one of his first executive actions on taking office.
President Trump strengthened it by adding additional reporting requirements for foreign-owned labs.
President Trump renewed it without changes after a six-month review by an advisory commission.
President Trump preserved the order but moved enforcement from NIST to the Department of Defense.
context: Frontier AI policy in the US has whipsawed between administrations. State-level rules (California, Texas), industry self-regulation, and de facto policy via export controls now do much of the work formal federal regulation does in Europe.

question: Andrej Karpathy was a founding member of OpenAI in 2015, then led Tesla's autopilot team for several years, then briefly returned to OpenAI before going independent. What is he best known for outside his employment history?
answer: Producing widely-shared educational content explaining neural networks and LLMs at the source-code level.
choices: Producing widely-shared educational content explaining neural networks and LLMs at the source-code level.
Founding a competing AI lab that received the largest seed funding round in Silicon Valley history.
Writing the original 2017 'Attention Is All You Need' paper that introduced the transformer.
Building the first commercial speech recognition system for industrial use in the early 2010s.
context: Karpathy's 'micrograd' tutorial — building a neural network library from scratch in a few hundred lines — and his lectures rebuilding GPT step by step are widely cited as some of the clearest technical explanations available.

question: Marvin Minsky co-founded the MIT AI Laboratory with John McCarthy in 1959. Beyond his 1969 Perceptrons book, what was his broader influence on the field?
answer: He shaped a generation of AI researchers as a charismatic and combative figure who championed symbolic over connectionist approaches.
choices: He shaped a generation of AI researchers as a charismatic and combative figure who championed symbolic over connectionist approaches.
He invented the LISP programming language at MIT and licensed it commercially to IBM.
He retired from research in 1969 to focus on philosophy of mind without further AI contributions.
He spent most of his career at Stanford working on robotics rather than AI proper.
context: Minsky's Society of Mind (1986) influenced cognitive science as much as AI. He died in 2016, just as the deep learning revolution he had helped delay was reshaping the field.

question: Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber published the foundational paper on Long Short-Term Memory networks in 1997. What problem did their architecture solve?
answer: The vanishing gradient problem in recurrent networks — LSTMs use gates to preserve information across many time steps.
choices: The vanishing gradient problem in recurrent networks — LSTMs use gates to preserve information across many time steps.
The exploding parameter problem — LSTMs compress weights by an order of magnitude during training.
The cold start problem in recommendation systems — LSTMs warm up cleanly without seed data.
The labelling problem in supervised learning — LSTMs work entirely without labels.
context: LSTMs dominated sequence modelling from the late 2000s until transformers replaced them in 2017. They are still used in some specialised settings — speech, time-series forecasting — but for language, transformers won decisively.

question: In 2015, OpenAI was founded as a non-profit by a group that included Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Ilya Sutskever, Greg Brockman, and others. The founding mission referenced a specific kind of structure. What was the original structure?
answer: Non-profit research organisation dedicated to building AGI safely for the benefit of all humanity.
choices: Non-profit research organisation dedicated to building AGI safely for the benefit of all humanity.
For-profit research lab funded by a consortium of US technology companies.
Government-affiliated research institute partly funded by the Department of Defense.
Academic partnership between Stanford and Carnegie Mellon universities.
context: By 2019, a 'capped-profit' arm was created to attract investment. By 2024, restructuring toward a full for-profit form was under public debate. The drift from the founding non-profit framing is a key part of OpenAI's governance story.

question: The transformer architecture's eight authors — Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser, Polosukhin — were all working at Google in 2017. What happened to most of them in the following years?
answer: They left Google and founded or joined competing AI startups, including Anthropic, Cohere, Character.AI, and others.
choices: They left Google and founded or joined competing AI startups, including Anthropic, Cohere, Character.AI, and others.
They all remained at Google Brain for the next decade as a tightly-knit research team.
They divided into two factions, one staying at Google and the other moving to Meta.
They abandoned AI research entirely and pursued other careers in academia and venture capital.
context: The 'brain drain' from Google — the company that invented the transformer — to its competitors is part of the larger story. Several authors became startup CEOs; the technology turned into an industry while its inventors moved on.

question: Andrew Karpathy's Tesla autopilot tenure (2017-2022) involved a specific technical decision that became controversial within the autonomous-vehicle community. What was the controversial choice?
answer: Tesla relied exclusively on cameras and neural networks, rejecting LIDAR sensors used by competitors like Waymo.
choices: Tesla relied exclusively on cameras and neural networks, rejecting LIDAR sensors used by competitors like Waymo.
Tesla used only LIDAR sensors and rejected cameras, the opposite of competitors' approach.
Tesla relied on roadside infrastructure rather than on-board sensors for navigation.
Tesla used only audio sensors and rejected both cameras and LIDAR.
context: The 'cameras only' bet was Musk's call. It works in some conditions and fails in others — fog, sun glare, unusual lighting. The trade-off between cost and safety in autonomy is real and ongoing.

question: DeepSeek, a Chinese AI lab affiliated with hedge fund High-Flyer, made headlines in early 2025 with a model trained at far lower cost than US frontier models — and released under open weights. What was the political significance of the release?
answer: It challenged the narrative that US export controls on chips would maintain a permanent American AI lead.
choices: It challenged the narrative that US export controls on chips would maintain a permanent American AI lead.
It confirmed that Chinese AI was at least a decade behind US frontier capabilities.
It demonstrated that closed-weights models would inevitably dominate the open-weights ones.
It proved that AI development outside California is not technically feasible.
context: DeepSeek's R1 model showed that strong reasoning could be built with clever engineering as well as raw compute spend. It also re-energised the open-source vs. closed-source debate at a politically sensitive moment.

question: Jürgen Schmidhuber, one of the inventors of LSTM, has spent his career arguing that he and others — particularly outside the US — invented much of modern deep learning earlier than the 'godfathers' are credited for. What is his general claim?
answer: Many key ideas — backpropagation, deep learning, generative models — were developed earlier in continental Europe than US-centric history admits.
choices: Many key ideas — backpropagation, deep learning, generative models — were developed earlier in continental Europe than US-centric history admits.
All of deep learning was invented by Schmidhuber's lab and the rest of the field has been derivative.
Deep learning is a fundamental break from earlier neural network work and owes nothing to it.
Deep learning was first developed at IBM in the 1960s and abandoned, then rediscovered.
context: Schmidhuber's specific historical claims have merit (LSTM's 1997 origins; early generative-network ideas in the 1990s). The broader complaint — that science history simplifies for convenience — is widely shared even by those who disagree on details.

question: DeepMind's AlphaFold predicts the three-dimensional structure of proteins from their amino acid sequence. By 2024 the freely-available AlphaFold database contained how many predicted structures?
answer: Over 200 million — covering essentially every protein known to science from across all species.
choices: Over 200 million — covering essentially every protein known to science from across all species.
About 50,000 — limited to clinically important human proteins relevant to drug discovery.
About 2 million — focused on bacterial and viral proteins for vaccine research.
About 10 billion — far more than the number of actually known proteins, including hypothetical variants.
context: Before AlphaFold, determining one protein structure took a PhD's worth of work — months of X-ray crystallography or cryo-EM. Now researchers download a prediction in seconds. This is the genuine scientific transformation the field has produced.

question: Diagnostic AI systems have been deployed in medical imaging — particularly in radiology, pathology, and ophthalmology. What is a representative real-world application?
answer: Detection of diabetic retinopathy from retinal photographs, FDA-cleared as an autonomous diagnostic device.
choices: Detection of diabetic retinopathy from retinal photographs, FDA-cleared as an autonomous diagnostic device.
Live brain-state reading during surgery to detect when a patient is in pain.
Predicting the timing of a heart attack a year in advance from saliva analysis.
Replacing radiologists entirely in 90% of US hospitals as of 2024.
context: IDx-DR was the first FDA-approved fully autonomous diagnostic AI (2018). Mammography, skin cancer detection, and pathology have similar systems. Augmentation of clinicians is now common; full replacement is not, despite a decade of predictions.

question: Google Translate's quality improved dramatically in 2016, when Google replaced its statistical phrase-based system with a new approach. What was the new approach?
answer: Neural machine translation — an encoder-decoder neural network that translates whole sentences rather than phrase fragments.
choices: Neural machine translation — an encoder-decoder neural network that translates whole sentences rather than phrase fragments.
Rule-based translation — a hand-coded grammar of every supported language pair, written by linguists.
Crowdsourced translation — every translation routed to a human in real time for verification.
Direct retrieval — searching a massive parallel corpus for the closest matching translation.
context: Neural MT roughly halved the gap between machine and human translation overnight for many language pairs. DeepL, founded the same year, pushed quality further. For major language pairs, modern translation is near-human for non-specialised text.

question: OpenAI's Whisper, released in September 2022 as open-source, is the most widely-used automatic speech recognition system in non-Big-Tech applications. What is the technical reason for its broad uptake?
answer: It was open-sourced under permissive license, multilingual out of the box, and accurate enough for production use without fine-tuning.
choices: It was open-sourced under permissive license, multilingual out of the box, and accurate enough for production use without fine-tuning.
It was kept proprietary but offered free for unlimited commercial use without restrictions.
It required no audio data at all, transcribing video by reading lip movements alone.
It was bundled with all major operating systems by 2023 and could not be uninstalled.
context: Whisper became the default ASR in many open-source pipelines. Combined with diffusion image generation and open LLMs, it is part of the open-source AI stack that operates as a counterweight to closed APIs.

question: ElevenLabs and similar services produce text-to-speech that is often indistinguishable from a specific human voice — given just a few minutes of training audio. What new risk does this create for ordinary people?
answer: Voice-clone scams — fraudsters impersonate family members on phone calls to extract money urgently.
choices: Voice-clone scams — fraudsters impersonate family members on phone calls to extract money urgently.
Singing competitions where AI voices compete with humans for music industry contracts.
Audio books taking five seconds to record instead of fifty hours.
Voice-based passwords being completely unbreakable from random users.
context: The defence is simple and worth setting up now: a family safe word agreed in person, never written down. If a voice 'sounds like grandma' begging for emergency money, ask for the word. No word, no money — even if the voice is perfect.

question: Recommendation systems on YouTube, TikTok, Netflix, and Spotify use AI to decide what to show each user next. What is the typical optimisation target — the thing the algorithm is trained to maximise?
answer: Engagement: watch time, click-through rate, return visits — proxies for user attention rather than for user wellbeing.
choices: Engagement: watch time, click-through rate, return visits — proxies for user attention rather than for user wellbeing.
Educational value — the algorithm prefers content that has been rated as informative by experts.
Random discovery — every user sees a uniform sample of all available content equally.
Producer revenue — the algorithm prefers content from creators who pay platform fees.
context: The trade-off is real: engagement metrics optimise for what holds your attention, not for what serves you. The bank's stance: this matters for kids who spend hours on these platforms, and the design choices are not neutral.

question: Weather forecasting has been disrupted by AI: Google's GraphCast and Huawei's Pangu-Weather can match or beat traditional numerical weather prediction (NWP). What is the substantive change?
answer: AI models trained on historical weather data run much faster than physics-based simulations while matching or exceeding accuracy on common metrics.
choices: AI models trained on historical weather data run much faster than physics-based simulations while matching or exceeding accuracy on common metrics.
AI models eliminate the need for any weather stations or satellites by predicting from first principles.
AI models work only for tropical regions and are useless for temperate-zone forecasting.
AI models replaced human meteorologists in every major broadcasting network by 2023.
context: This is a clear-cut case where deep learning produced real scientific progress in an established field. GraphCast in particular has been integrated into operational forecasts at multiple weather services. The future is likely hybrid — AI plus physics.

question: AI in drug discovery — Insilico Medicine, Atomwise, Recursion, Exscientia — uses neural networks to identify candidate molecules. What part of the drug development pipeline does this most plausibly speed up?
answer: Early candidate identification and lead optimisation; the expensive clinical trials still dominate total cost and time.
choices: Early candidate identification and lead optimisation; the expensive clinical trials still dominate total cost and time.
Manufacturing of approved drugs at industrial scale, replacing chemical engineers.
Regulatory approval at the FDA, replacing the review process entirely.
Patient recruitment for clinical trials, eliminating the need for any human participants.
context: AI has produced a handful of clinical-trial-stage candidates. The end-to-end claim — 'AI will design the next blockbuster drug from scratch' — has not yet been demonstrated. The realistic claim — 'AI speeds up parts of the pipeline' — is well-supported.

question: Precision agriculture uses AI in several ways. One representative application combines satellite imagery and on-tractor sensors. What does the AI typically decide?
answer: Where to apply fertiliser, pesticide, or water — adjusting in real time across a field by square metre rather than uniformly.
choices: Where to apply fertiliser, pesticide, or water — adjusting in real time across a field by square metre rather than uniformly.
Whether a farm should grow corn or wheat — by analysing global market data alone.
Which farm workers to hire or fire based on biometric productivity scoring.
Which crops to ban from a region under federal regulations enforced by satellite.
context: Precision agriculture saves real resources — water, chemicals, fuel — when deployed well. Concerns: vendor lock-in, data ownership questions, and disparate impact on smaller farms unable to afford the equipment.

question: Capability and consciousness are routinely conflated in AI coverage. A specific 2022 incident — when Google engineer Blake Lemoine claimed the company's LaMDA chatbot was sentient — became the textbook case for confusing them. What was the outcome?
answer: Lemoine was placed on leave and then fired. LaMDA was not, by any defensible standard, sentient.
choices: Lemoine was placed on leave and then fired. LaMDA was not, by any defensible standard, sentient.
Lemoine was promoted to lead Google's consciousness research division.
LaMDA was formally recognised as a sentient being under California law in 2023.
The story turned out to be a hoax — there was no engineer named Lemoine.
context: The bank's stance: capability is real and impressive; consciousness claims about LLMs remain wildly overblown. Read patterns out, do not read minds into. LaMDA was a sophisticated next-token predictor, not a person.

question: OpenAI's Sora (announced 2024) and Google's Veo are video-generation models. What is the basic technical challenge that distinguishes video generation from still-image generation?
answer: Temporal coherence — keeping objects, characters, and physics consistent across many frames is much harder than single-image consistency.
choices: Temporal coherence — keeping objects, characters, and physics consistent across many frames is much harder than single-image consistency.
Audio synchronisation — videos must include audio, and lip-sync requires perfect coordination with the visual.
Compression — videos are physically too large to fit on any modern hard drive.
Resolution — video resolution must match the highest available cinema screen, requiring eight times normal compute.
context: A character who looks identical in frame 1 and frame 60, with consistent clothing and shadows, is hard. Specific physics — water, fire, falling objects — remains shaky. Video generation in 2024 produces stunning seconds, less reliable minutes.

question: A novel translation use of LLMs: localising video game dialogue across dozens of languages. What is the practical gain compared to traditional human translation?
answer: Speed and cost — a first-pass translation can be produced in hours rather than weeks, then refined by human editors.
choices: Speed and cost — a first-pass translation can be produced in hours rather than weeks, then refined by human editors.
Quality — LLMs always produce better translations than human translators in every language pair.
Privacy — LLMs do not see the text, only its statistical signature.
Legal protection — LLM translations are exempt from copyright restrictions on the original.
context: The human-in-the-loop workflow is the realistic deployment. LLM-only translation still produces errors that careful human review catches. The cost reduction is real but quality assurance has not been eliminated.

question: A 2023 study by GitHub measured developer productivity using Copilot. What did the study most carefully establish?
answer: Developers using Copilot completed a benchmark task notably faster, with self-reported quality similar to control.
choices: Developers using Copilot completed a benchmark task notably faster, with self-reported quality similar to control.
Developers using Copilot produced code with 80% fewer bugs than developers without it.
Developers using Copilot completed tasks ten times faster on every benchmark studied.
Developers using Copilot earned higher salaries within six months of installation.
context: Real-world productivity is harder to measure than benchmark tasks. The honest summary: useful tool, real gains for many engineers, no replacement of the engineer's judgment.

question: Deepfake video — a person's face swapped onto another body's footage — has gotten convincing for short clips. What visual cues still betray many deepfakes in 2024 to a careful viewer?
answer: Inconsistent blinking, edge fuzz where the face meets the hair, mouth-sync drift, and lighting that does not match the scene.
choices: Inconsistent blinking, edge fuzz where the face meets the hair, mouth-sync drift, and lighting that does not match the scene.
Deepfake videos are always silent because audio cannot be cloned.
Deepfake videos are always black and white because colour generation has not been solved.
Deepfake videos always have a visible watermark in the upper right corner.
context: These tells will not last. Detection-by-eye is a temporary advantage and an evolving art. Combine with context — does the speaker say plausible things, from a plausible setting, on a verified channel — for stronger judgement.

question: When evaluating an AI-generated image of a person, several specific features in the image often reveal the artifice — even in late-2024 generators. What features?
answer: Hands with the wrong finger count, jewellery blending into skin, garbled text on signs, asymmetric earrings, melting watch faces.
choices: Hands with the wrong finger count, jewellery blending into skin, garbled text on signs, asymmetric earrings, melting watch faces.
Watermarks deliberately inserted by the AI provider to mark generated images for detection.
Mandatory black bars across the bottom required by federal law since 2023.
Numerical timestamps in the upper-left corner indicating generation time.
context: Hand-counting has been a deepfake reliable tell for two years and is getting harder. Text in images and complex compositional details (mirrors, reflections, complex jewellery) are the next holdouts. The arms race continues; spot-checking remains worthwhile.

question: A common pattern in AI-written text exhibits certain stylistic tells: heavy em-dash use, fondness for tricolons ('A, B, and C'), stock metaphors like 'tapestry of', 'delve into', 'navigate the landscape', and 'in the realm of'. What practical use can a reader make of these tells?
answer: Treat them as weak cues that prompt verification of facts and claims, not as conclusive proof of AI authorship.
choices: Treat them as weak cues that prompt verification of facts and claims, not as conclusive proof of AI authorship.
Treat them as definitive proof of AI authorship and discard the text immediately.
Treat them as evidence the writer is highly educated and trust the claims more.
Treat them as a watermark mandated by the AI provider and conclude the text is reliable.
context: Human writers use these patterns too. The honest practice: when a document feels AI-flavoured, verify the load-bearing claims. The cues are signals, not proofs — and they will fade as model training diversifies.

question: Clearview AI, the facial recognition company founded by Hoan Ton-That, built one of the largest face databases in the world by scraping billions of photos from social media and the open web. Roughly how many photos has the company claimed to hold by 2023?
answer: Over 30 billion photos scraped from social media, news sites, and other public sources without explicit consent.
choices: Over 30 billion photos scraped from social media, news sites, and other public sources without explicit consent.
About 100,000 photos legally licensed from individuals and stock photo agencies.
About one million photos purchased from major social media companies.
About 500 photos hand-collected by Clearview employees from public records.
context: Clearview's customer list reportedly included thousands of police departments, ICE, and some private firms. Multiple countries (UK, France, Italy, Australia) have ruled the scraping illegal under their privacy laws. Your face is in the database whether you consent or not.

question: When verifying an AI's factual claim — say, 'Frederick Douglass gave a speech in Rochester on July 4, 1852' — what is the most reliable single-step check for an ordinary user?
answer: Search a reliable external source — Wikipedia, the original archive, a major newspaper's index — rather than asking another AI.
choices: Search a reliable external source — Wikipedia, the original archive, a major newspaper's index — rather than asking another AI.
Ask the same AI again to confirm itself, since repeated answers are always correct.
Accept the claim if the AI sounds confident, since confidence correlates with truth.
Trust the AI completely; checking is paranoid and wastes time.
context: Multiple-AI comparison is also useful — if two systems disagree, you have a flag worth investigating. But for hard facts, an external source is the gold standard. AI is not a fact engine; it is a language engine.

question: AI math errors are unreliable in a specific dangerous way: they produce confident-looking wrong answers. What is the practical defence when using AI for any arithmetic that matters?
answer: Verify with a calculator or spreadsheet, or have the AI use a calculator tool, before acting on any computed number.
choices: Verify with a calculator or spreadsheet, or have the AI use a calculator tool, before acting on any computed number.
Trust the AI completely; calculator tools are unnecessary for modern systems.
Multiply every answer by two as a safety margin before acting on it.
Ignore arithmetic entirely; only use AI for free-form writing.
context: Modern frontier models use a calculator tool when available, which dramatically improves arithmetic. Without it, expect errors. Always sanity-check the math the AI does, especially when stakes are real (tax, medication doses, financial planning).

question: An LLM trained on the internet has likely absorbed material from countless copyrighted books, articles, and codebases without explicit licensing. What practical advice follows for users producing original work with AI help?
answer: Treat AI-generated text as draft material to be substantially rewritten and verified, not as final content to publish without review.
choices: Treat AI-generated text as draft material to be substantially rewritten and verified, not as final content to publish without review.
Submit AI-generated text directly without modification, since it is automatically considered original work.
Avoid all AI use to prevent accidental copyright infringement.
Pay a flat fee to OpenAI to cover any copyright claims arising from generated text.
context: Distinct concerns: provenance of training data is one debate. The user's own publication of AI text is another. Verify facts, attribute sources, rewrite substantially — these are the working habits that keep the user clean regardless of how the training-data debate resolves.

question: Voice-clone scams target the elderly specifically. What is the typical urgency pattern scammers use to bypass careful verification?
answer: Pretending the grandchild is in immediate physical danger or legal trouble that requires money in the next hour.
choices: Pretending the grandchild is in immediate physical danger or legal trouble that requires money in the next hour.
Slowly building rapport over several weeks before mentioning money at all.
Sending the relative a long written letter explaining the situation in detail.
Hosting a videoconference with the relative's whole family present.
context: Urgency is the operative weapon. The defence is also operative: slow down, hang up, verify on a known number, require the safe word. Scams collapse under five minutes of friction; that is why they push for ten seconds of decision.

question: If your face has appeared in any reasonably public photo on the internet — yearbook, news article, friend's social post — it is almost certainly in some facial recognition database. What can a person realistically do about this?
answer: Submit opt-out requests where companies provide them (Clearview, PimEyes), but accept that complete removal is largely unachievable.
choices: Submit opt-out requests where companies provide them (Clearview, PimEyes), but accept that complete removal is largely unachievable.
Issue a single federal request that erases your face from every database.
Wear sunglasses every time you appear in any photograph.
Sue every database operator individually for a guaranteed multi-million-dollar settlement.
context: Some EU residents have rights that can force removal. US options are weaker. The realistic posture: limit voluntary face uploads to public services (avoid social media profile photos that scrape easily), and assume your face is already in the wild.

question: A phishing email that includes the recipient's name, employer, and recent purchase history is more convincing than a generic one. How does generative AI change phishing economics?
answer: It makes personalised, contextually accurate phishing cheap at scale, removing the grammatical errors that used to be a giveaway.
choices: It makes personalised, contextually accurate phishing cheap at scale, removing the grammatical errors that used to be a giveaway.
It makes phishing entirely impossible for technical reasons.
It is regulated by US law and cannot be used for phishing under any circumstances.
It only generates phishing emails in obscure languages no one reads.
context: The 'bad grammar' tell is largely gone. The defence shifts to verifying out of band (call the sender on a known number), checking links carefully, and being skeptical of any urgent request. The threat surface has widened; the principles still apply.

question: A 'data minimisation' approach to using AI for personal questions involves a specific practical move. What is it?
answer: Asking your question without unnecessary personal context — share only what is needed for the answer.
choices: Asking your question without unnecessary personal context — share only what is needed for the answer.
Sharing as much personal context as possible to get a better answer.
Asking the question on someone else's account.
Asking the question in a different language than your own.
context: If asking 'what should I cook tonight?', you do not need to include your full address, kids' names, allergies, or family history of heart disease — unless the question literally requires them. Default to minimum, not maximum.

question: AI-powered translation can subtly mistranslate sensitive content — medical terms, legal phrases, religious texts. What is the practical safeguard?
answer: Back-translate (translate the output back to the source language) and compare to the original to catch obvious mistakes.
choices: Back-translate (translate the output back to the source language) and compare to the original to catch obvious mistakes.
Trust the AI translation completely under all circumstances.
Translate only into English, as English is the only reliable target language.
Use a different AI service for every translation to avoid bias.
context: Back-translation is a real working technique. For high-stakes translation (medical consent forms, legal contracts), a certified human translator is still required. Use AI for first drafts and triage, not for final outputs in life-affecting domains.

question: Several major AI companies offer 'enterprise' tiers with explicit no-train commitments and data-residency guarantees. What does this signal about the consumer tier?
answer: The consumer tier almost certainly trains on user data by default — paid privacy is a real product feature, not an unexpected upsell.
choices: The consumer tier almost certainly trains on user data by default — paid privacy is a real product feature, not an unexpected upsell.
The enterprise tier is identical to the consumer tier in all data-handling respects.
The enterprise tier is more expensive but technically inferior.
The enterprise tier is exclusively for users in the European Union.
context: Read the policies. The structure says: 'You can choose; this is the tier where we offer the contractual commitment'. For sensitive use, the enterprise tier — or a local model — is the right choice.

question: The Department of Homeland Security briefly stood up a 'Disinformation Governance Board' in April 2022. What happened?
answer: Public backlash and 'Ministry of Truth' comparisons led to its suspension within weeks and formal disbanding by August.
choices: Public backlash and 'Ministry of Truth' comparisons led to its suspension within weeks and formal disbanding by August.
It is still in operation as of 2024 and has classified over a million pieces of content.
It was renamed and continues as the National Truth Authority.
It was merged with the National Weather Service.
context: Nina Jankowicz was its short-lived director. The episode is a useful case study: the politics of who decides what is true matter as much as the technology. The infrastructure for institutional 'truth' verdicts is not a settled question.

question: Behavioural nudging — Cass Sunstein and Richard Thaler's 2008 book *Nudge* — proposed that 'choice architects' could influence behaviour without restricting choice. What capability does AI add to nudging at scale?
answer: Personalisation: each person can receive a nudge calibrated to their psychological profile, A/B-tested on outcomes.
choices: Personalisation: each person can receive a nudge calibrated to their psychological profile, A/B-tested on outcomes.
Free pizza for everyone who participates in a nudge programme.
Mandatory participation in any nudge programme decided by federal regulators.
Complete elimination of all marketing across the internet.
context: Sunstein's framing — 'libertarian paternalism' — assumed the nudger was a benign actor. AI scales the technique to ad-targeting, content moderation, and platform UI. Whether 'nudging' shades into manipulation depends on what is being nudged toward and by whom.

question: Insurance underwriting increasingly uses AI risk-scoring on data sources well beyond what a person consciously discloses — social media activity, purchase patterns, even genomic information in some lines. What is the practical concern for ordinary policyholders?
answer: Risk pricing becomes finer-grained, but transparency is often weak — denied or expensive coverage with limited appeal.
choices: Risk pricing becomes finer-grained, but transparency is often weak — denied or expensive coverage with limited appeal.
Insurance has been universally abolished as of 2024.
Insurance pricing is unrelated to any data analytics.
Insurance companies are required to share their full models with every customer.
context: Insurance has been actuarial since the seventeenth century; the AI shift is in granularity and opacity. State regulators have varied responses. As a consumer, knowing what data flows into your scoring is part of basic financial literacy.

question: Predictive policing — PredPol (later 'Geolitica') and competitors — uses AI to forecast where crime will occur and direct patrol resources. What is the recurring critique from civil liberties groups?
answer: Models trained on historical arrest data reinforce existing patrol patterns in over-policed neighbourhoods, amplifying bias.
choices: Models trained on historical arrest data reinforce existing patrol patterns in over-policed neighbourhoods, amplifying bias.
Predictive policing has eliminated all crime in cities that use it.
Predictive policing is illegal under federal law and not used by any department.
Predictive policing uses no data and is purely intuition-based.
context: LAPD discontinued PredPol use in 2020 amid Stop LAPD Spying coalition pressure. Other departments continue. The disparate-impact concern is real and structural: feedback loops between policing and data are hard to disentangle.

question: What is the practical reason a 'safe word' rather than a security question is the right primary defence against voice-clone scams targeting family?
answer: Security questions (mother's maiden name, first pet) are scrapeable from social media; a safe word is private by design.
choices: Security questions (mother's maiden name, first pet) are scrapeable from social media; a safe word is private by design.
Safe words are illegal in many US states.
Security questions are universally agreed to be the strongest form of authentication.
Safe words can be guessed by trying random English words.
