context: Torres, formerly an EA insider, has become a leading critic. Cremer and Kemp's 2021 'Democratising Risk' paper challenged the techno-utopian frame and met heavy resistance from EA leadership.

question: On March 2018, leaked details revealed Google was helping the Pentagon's Project Maven analyze drone surveillance footage with AI. More than 4,000 Google employees signed an open letter to CEO Sundar Pichai. About a dozen resigned. By June 2018, Google announced it would not renew the contract. What broader principle emerged from this episode?
answer: Tech workers, briefly, held real leverage over their employers' military contracts — a leverage that subsequent companies have moved to limit through stricter speech and contracting policies.
choices: Tech workers, briefly, held real leverage over their employers' military contracts — a leverage that subsequent companies have moved to limit through stricter speech and contracting policies.
Google was permanently barred from Department of Defense contracts by federal injunction in June 2018, ending the matter.
Project Maven was never real; the leak was a hoax, and no employees actually resigned over the matter.
Google immediately replaced all employees who signed the letter, demonstrating that worker activism has no power in the tech industry.
context: Google updated its AI principles afterward to bar weapons applications. By 2024, Google had taken on new Pentagon contracts; subsequent employee protests had less effect, with terminations following speak-outs.

question: DeepSeek-R1 was released open-source by a Chinese lab on January 23, 2025. On January 27, NVIDIA's stock dropped roughly 17%, wiping about $589 billion off its market cap in a single day — the largest one-day value loss for any company in history. What about R1's release triggered this magnitude of market reaction?
answer: It matched o1-class reasoning at a fraction of reported training cost, with weights freely available, undercutting the premise.
choices: It matched o1-class reasoning at a fraction of reported training cost, with weights freely available, undercutting the premise.
DeepSeek announced it would never use NVIDIA chips again, immediately removing its forecast demand from analyst models.
DeepSeek-R1 was found to be a copy of NVIDIA's internal model, leading to a fraud investigation by the SEC.
DeepSeek's launch coincided with a planned NVIDIA earnings miss already priced in by analysts before the release.
context: DeepSeek's reported training cost (~$6M for V3-base) drew skepticism but the open release was real. NVIDIA's stock recovered within months; the structural question about inference vs. training compute remains open.

question: Pegasus is spyware developed by Israel's NSO Group. Once installed, it can read messages, listen via the microphone, watch via the camera, and silently exfiltrate data. The 2021 Pegasus Project found targeting of journalists at the NYT, WSJ, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, and Le Monde. What infection technique made Pegasus especially dangerous on iPhones?
answer: Zero-click exploits delivered through iMessage and other channels could compromise the device with no user interaction at all, leaving no warning sign on the phone.
choices: Zero-click exploits delivered through iMessage and other channels could compromise the device with no user interaction at all, leaving no warning sign on the phone.
Phishing emails required the target to click a malicious link, which was easy to defeat with basic email awareness training.
Physical access to the device was required, so targets could simply refuse to hand over their phones to be infected.
Pegasus only worked on jailbroken iPhones, so any user keeping their device updated was fully safe from infection.
context: Apple sued NSO Group in November 2021. Citizen Lab and Amnesty's Security Lab have repeatedly documented Pegasus on journalists and activists in Jordan, India, Mexico, and elsewhere.

question: AlphaFold 2, from DeepMind, predicted protein structures at near-experimental accuracy in 2020. By 2024 the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database had grown to over 200 million entries — essentially the entire known proteome. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with David Baker. What did the open release of these predictions actually change?
answer: Researchers worldwide gained free access to a structural starting point for almost any protein they study, collapsing months of crystallography work into a database lookup.
choices: Researchers worldwide gained free access to a structural starting point for almost any protein they study, collapsing months of crystallography work into a database lookup.
AlphaFold replaced all wet-lab biology, with X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM facilities closing worldwide by 2024.
Predictions were paywalled and licensed only to pharmaceutical giants, deepening the divide between rich and poor labs.
Predictions were proven incorrect for over 90% of proteins, leading the Nobel committee to rescind the 2024 prize.
context: Joint Nobel Chemistry 2024: Hassabis and Jumper for AlphaFold; David Baker for computational protein design (Rosetta, RFdiffusion). The 2024 Physics Nobel went to Hopfield and Hinton.

question: ARC-AGI, a benchmark designed by François Chollet in 2019, presents abstract visual reasoning puzzles built to resist memorization: each grid task is novel. Through 2023 even GPT-4 scored low; in late 2024 a private OpenAI o3 configuration reportedly scored around 76% on the public set. What pattern of result does this represent for the 'AGI' debate?
answer: Targeted reasoning training plus massive inference compute can push scores on abstraction-heavy benchmarks rapidly, but the cost-per-task and out-of-distribution generalization.
choices: Targeted reasoning training plus massive inference compute can push scores on abstraction-heavy benchmarks rapidly, but the cost-per-task and out-of-distribution generalization.
ARC-AGI has been fully saturated since 2022; any model that fails it is considered defective by industry standards.
ARC-AGI is a parlor trick with no relationship to general intelligence and was retired by Chollet in early 2024.
ARC-AGI is identical to MMLU; the two are interchangeable benchmarks used by labs to inflate marketing claims.
context: Chollet kept the test set private to resist contamination. The o3 result cost reportedly thousands of dollars per task to compute. 'AGI' claims hinge on both score and economics.

question: A 'prompt injection' attack puts malicious instructions inside content the AI processes — a webpage, an email, a PDF — instead of in the user's typed prompt. The AI, processing that content, treats the embedded instructions as commands. Why is this called the 'SQL injection of the AI era,' and why is it so hard to fully fix?
answer: LLMs cannot reliably separate trusted instructions from untrusted data within the same context window, so any user-fetched content is a potential channel for hidden commands.
choices: LLMs cannot reliably separate trusted instructions from untrusted data within the same context window, so any user-fetched content is a potential channel for hidden commands.
Prompt injection only works on small models under 1B parameters; frontier models are immune by training data exposure alone.
Prompt injection requires physical access to the AI's GPU and so cannot occur over the network in practice.
Prompt injection has been solved since 2023 by a regex filter that every major lab now ships by default.
context: Simon Willison popularized the term in 2022. Indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al. 2023) embeds instructions in webpages, search results, or shared documents. Mitigation is partial — strict separation, sandboxing — but not full.

question: 'Jailbreaks' have evolved from the 2023 DAN prompts ('Do Anything Now') and 'grandma' role-plays to more systematic techniques: encoding harmful asks in base64, multi-turn manipulation, persona attacks, automated red-team generators like PAIR. Why are reliable, persistent jailbreak defenses still elusive in 2024-2025 frontier models?
answer: Safety training adjusts output distributions on examples it has seen; adversaries with creative attack surfaces keep finding inputs that fall outside that distribution and bypass the refusal pattern.
choices: Safety training adjusts output distributions on examples it has seen; adversaries with creative attack surfaces keep finding inputs that fall outside that distribution and bypass the refusal pattern.
Jailbreaks are fully solved; every major lab ships a model that cannot be jailbroken by any known attack as of late 2023.
Jailbreaks only target image models, so text chatbots are inherently safe from this entire category of attack.
Jailbreaks are too compute-intensive for any attacker to attempt, so they remain a theoretical concern with no real-world examples.
context: Red-team economics favor attackers: one new bypass beats many trained refusals. Anthropic's CHARM and OpenAI's Preparedness teams ship continuous patches but never claim full coverage.

question: Voice cloning models — ElevenLabs, OpenAI's Voice Engine, open-weight Tortoise — can replicate a target voice from a few seconds of audio. 'Grandparent scams' now feature cloned voices of grandchildren in distress, asking for wire transfers. What practical defense, costing nothing, blunts this entire class of attack at the family level?
answer: A pre-agreed family safe word, known only to family members, that the caller must produce on demand; no real grandchild forgets it, no clone can guess it.
choices: A pre-agreed family safe word, known only to family members, that the caller must produce on demand; no real grandchild forgets it, no clone can guess it.
Carrying an FCC-certified voice authentication device that family members swap into the call to verify identity.
Trusting caller ID, which voice cloning cannot manipulate and which always reflects the true origin of the call.
Refusing all calls from unknown numbers, since voice cloning only works from blocked or private caller IDs.
context: FTC consumer alerts now name voice cloning explicitly. Some banks require callback to a known number, but family-level defenses (safe word, callback to a known landline) close the gap fastest.

question: Deepfake videos are now produced by consumer tools — HeyGen, Synthesia, Wav2Lip. Detection is an arms race: each new generator quickly trains classifiers to identify it, and new generators evade them. For a non-technical viewer, what cues remain most useful even as quality improves in 2024-2025?
answer: Mismatched lip-sync timing on plosives, inconsistent reflections in eyes or glasses, hand and finger anomalies, and audio that does not match the room's acoustics in the video.
choices: Mismatched lip-sync timing on plosives, inconsistent reflections in eyes or glasses, hand and finger anomalies, and audio that does not match the room's acoustics in the video.
Any video older than five minutes is automatically a real recording, since deepfake tools can only handle short clips.
Detection apps in iOS or Android always identify deepfakes with 100% accuracy at the moment of playback.
Watermarks visible to the naked eye are required by federal law on all AI-generated video as of 2024.
context: C2PA content credentials offer cryptographic provenance, but adoption is partial and watermarks can be stripped. Behavioral verification (back-channel callbacks, asking for a specific gesture) remains the strongest defense.

question: When you paste a confidential document into a free AI chatbot, what typically happens to that content depends on the provider's policy and tier. For free consumer ChatGPT, Gemini, and similar services, what is the default fate of your conversations as of 2024-2025?
answer: Conversations are retained and may be used to train future models unless you affirmatively opt out, which the provider often makes available but rarely puts in front of users.
choices: Conversations are retained and may be used to train future models unless you affirmatively opt out, which the provider often makes available but rarely puts in front of users.
Conversations are deleted instantly after the session ends and never reach the provider's servers.
Conversations are encrypted with a key only the user holds, so the provider cannot read them under any circumstances.
Conversations are protected by HIPAA and GDPR by default in all consumer tiers, regardless of jurisdiction.
context: Enterprise tiers (ChatGPT Enterprise, Anthropic's commercial API) typically default to no-training. Consumer free tiers default to training-eligible. Always read the actual policy for your tier.

question: Many schools deploy AI surveillance products — Gaggle, GoGuardian, Bark, Lightspeed Alert — that scan student email, chat, browser history, and sometimes camera feeds for keywords indicating self-harm, violence, or 'concerning' content. Beyond civil-liberties concerns, what specific operational failure mode have these products demonstrated repeatedly?
answer: High false-positive rates flag innocuous content — book reports on classic literature, LGBTQ resources, discussions of mental health.
choices: High false-positive rates flag innocuous content — book reports on classic literature, LGBTQ resources, discussions of mental health.
Perfect accuracy with no false positives, but at a cost so high that no district can afford to deploy them.
Inability to scan English text, which means they only function in foreign-language schools.
Federal law forbids their use in K-12, so the products are sold but never actually deployed in any school district.
context: Pew, EFF, and 74 reporting have documented hundreds of false-positive police contacts. The products work by keyword and sentiment, not by understanding intent.

question: Pasting personal information into a chatbot — full name, date of birth, employer, medical history, an upcoming travel schedule — is now common practice. Even when the provider promises 'no training,' what residual data risk remains that careful users plan around?
answer: Logs persist for abuse-monitoring and legal-compliance windows; subpoenas, breaches, or future policy shifts can expose data retained under those carve-outs.
choices: Logs persist for abuse-monitoring and legal-compliance windows; subpoenas, breaches, or future policy shifts can expose data retained under those carve-outs.
No residual risk at all; 'no training' contracts include cryptographic guarantees of instant deletion across every server.
The model itself memorizes every conversation it sees, regardless of training settings, and can be queried for any prior session.
The data is transferred only by hand-delivered USB drives that are physically destroyed after each session.
context: OpenAI's API ToS retain logs for 30 days for abuse monitoring even with training off. Court orders have required temporary preservation in litigation. Local models avoid this category entirely.

question: AI-driven phishing now produces grammatically perfect, contextually accurate emails targeting specific individuals, often referencing real recent events from the target's social media. Cybersecurity researchers report click rates significantly above traditional phishing baselines. What technical practice — not a chatbot lecture — most reliably blunts the attack?
answer: Hardware security keys (YubiKey, Titan) for multi-factor authentication, requiring a physical token that cannot be replayed even on a perfect phish.
choices: Hardware security keys (YubiKey, Titan) for multi-factor authentication, requiring a physical token that cannot be replayed even on a perfect phish.
SMS-based 2FA, which has been mathematically proven immune to AI-driven attacks of all kinds.
Memorizing a longer password, which alone defeats both classical and AI-driven phishing attempts.
Switching browsers daily, which prevents AI from learning your browsing habits over time.
context: FIDO2/WebAuthn standards underlie hardware keys. SMS 2FA is vulnerable to SIM-swap attacks. Password managers plus hardware keys form the practical defense in depth.

question: AI 'agents' that browse the web for the user — Operator, Computer Use, Manus — extend the prompt-injection threat surface dramatically. The agent can read mail, fill forms, click buttons, transfer money. What is the most basic risk-reduction principle for any agent deployment, regardless of vendor?
answer: Least-privilege scoping per task: give the agent the minimum tools it needs for this job, require human approval before consequential actions, and bound the time and data it can access.
choices: Least-privilege scoping per task: give the agent the minimum tools it needs for this job, require human approval before consequential actions, and bound the time and data it can access.
Maximum-privilege scoping per task: give the agent full account access so it can complete any chained action without friction.
No scoping at all: agents must run with root permissions on all systems they touch, since restricted permissions cause failures.
Random scoping per task: agents must select their own permissions, which prevents human error from limiting their capabilities.
context: Agent frameworks routinely violate the principle. Anthropic's computer-use docs and OpenAI's Operator both warn about prompt-injection risk explicitly; uptake of explicit allowlists is the gap.

question: AI-generated images carry telltales that survive most casual viewing: anatomical errors in hands, jewelry blending into skin, signs that read as gibberish at high zoom, eye-reflection inconsistencies. By late 2024, the latest models had reduced but not eliminated these. What separately verifiable check is more reliable than any visual cue for high-stakes claims?
answer: Reverse-image search and provenance tracing: Google Images, TinEye, and C2PA credentials reveal whether the image existed before today and where it actually came from.
choices: Reverse-image search and provenance tracing: Google Images, TinEye, and C2PA credentials reveal whether the image existed before today and where it actually came from.
Asking the chatbot that produced it whether it is real, since AI is mathematically required to be truthful about its own outputs.
Magnifying the image to 1000x and looking for individual pixels, which always reveals whether an image is AI-generated.
Checking the image's file extension, since AI-generated images always use .ai or .gpt extensions.
context: C2PA is gaining adoption (Adobe, Microsoft, BBC). Adversaries strip credentials trivially. Reverse search defeats most reused or recycled AI images on first attempt.

question: Browser extensions that integrate with AI services can read or modify any webpage you visit, including form contents and authentication tokens. A malicious or compromised AI-integration extension could exfiltrate everything you type. What permission hygiene catches most of the risk before installation?
answer: Inspect the extension's listed permissions; reject any extension that requests 'read and change all data' on every website unless you can fully audit the publisher.
choices: Inspect the extension's listed permissions; reject any extension that requests 'read and change all data' on every website unless you can fully audit the publisher.
Trust extensions equally if they have over 100,000 users, since popularity guarantees safety in browser stores.
Install all extensions promoted on social media, since algorithmic ranking guarantees the safest options reach the top.
Enable all permissions on all extensions, since browser sandboxes mathematically prevent any malicious behavior.
context: Chrome Web Store has repeatedly removed extensions caught exfiltrating data. The trust chain is the publisher's identity plus update integrity, neither of which the store fully verifies.

question: California SB 1047, the Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier AI Models Act, would have required developers of large covered models to implement a full-shutdown capability, submit a written safety protocol, retain a third-party annual auditor, and accept liability for 'critical harms.' Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed it on September 29, 2024. What was his core stated objection?
answer: The bill set stringent standards based on training cost and compute scale rather than empirical risk in deployment, potentially regulating basic functions while missing smaller, specialized models.
choices: The bill set stringent standards based on training cost and compute scale rather than empirical risk in deployment, potentially regulating basic functions while missing smaller, specialized models.
The bill would have violated the US Constitution's interstate commerce clause, making veto compulsory rather than discretionary.
The bill required a 100% shutdown of all AI activity in California, which the Governor judged economically catastrophic.
The bill had no meaningful content; the veto was procedural and could be reissued in identical form the following year.
context: Newsom's letter cited the absence of 'empirical evidence and science.' Critics on both sides claimed regulatory capture: incumbents could have absorbed costs while open-source labs and small developers could not.

question: The EU AI Act entered into force on August 1, 2024, with a tiered risk approach: 'unacceptable risk' practices banned outright, 'high-risk' systems heavily regulated, 'limited risk' with transparency duties, and 'minimal risk' essentially unregulated. The unacceptable list took effect in February 2025. What practice is among the explicitly banned 'unacceptable' uses?
answer: Social scoring systems that evaluate or classify natural persons over time based on social behavior or inferred personality, leading to unjustified detrimental treatment.
choices: Social scoring systems that evaluate or classify natural persons over time based on social behavior or inferred personality, leading to unjustified detrimental treatment.
Any LLM with more than one billion parameters, regardless of how it is trained or deployed in member states.
All facial recognition, including private uses in homes or for personal device unlock features.
Generative AI for any purpose, with mandatory shutdown of all chatbots in EU member states from August 2024.
context: Other banned practices include untargeted face-image scraping, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools, certain biometric categorization, and real-time public biometric ID for law enforcement (with narrow exceptions). Penalties: up to €40M or 7% of global turnover.

question: Joe Biden signed Executive Order 14110 on October 30, 2023, titled 'Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence.' It directed NIST to set standards, required reporting from large training runs, and named more than fifty federal agency tasks. On his first day, January 20, 2025, Donald Trump rescinded it. What did Trump issue in its place three days later?
answer: Executive Order 'Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence,' aimed at accelerating US AI development free from what it called 'ideological.
choices: Executive Order 'Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence,' aimed at accelerating US AI development free from what it called 'ideological.
Executive Order ratifying the Bletchley Park Declaration as binding US law on all domestic AI developers.
Executive Order banning all AI training in the United States above a 10B-parameter threshold.
Executive Order transferring AI oversight authority from NIST to the Department of Education.
context: The Jan 23 EO directed the Office of Science and Technology Policy to develop an action plan within 180 days. The shift signals a US policy pivot away from precautionary framing toward growth-first.

question: The Bletchley Park AI Safety Summit was hosted by the UK government on November 1-2, 2023. Twenty-eight countries signed the Bletchley Declaration, including the United States, China, India, the EU, and African states. What concrete commitment did the Declaration include?
answer: An agreement to identify shared AI safety risks and develop risk-based national policies cooperatively.
choices: An agreement to identify shared AI safety risks and develop risk-based national policies cooperatively.
A binding treaty to pause all frontier AI training globally until international standards were ratified.
Mandatory NIST oversight of all signatory states' AI labs, with enforcement teeth under UK jurisdiction.
Immediate dissolution of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind under a multinational governance accord.
context: Subsequent summits (Seoul May 2024, Paris February 2025) continued the dialogue. The structural critique: declarations create the appearance of governance without the substance; firms regulate themselves under cover of consultation.

question: On October 7, 2019, the US Department of Commerce added 28 Chinese entities to the Entity List, restricting them from buying US-origin components. Among them: Hikvision, Dahua Technology, SenseTime, Megvii, iFlytek. What specifically did the State Department cite as the basis for the listing?
answer: Their role in China's campaign of mass surveillance, arbitrary detention, and high-tech monitoring of Uyghurs, Kazakhs, and other Muslim minorities in Xinjiang.
choices: Their role in China's campaign of mass surveillance, arbitrary detention, and high-tech monitoring of Uyghurs, Kazakhs, and other Muslim minorities in Xinjiang.
Their failure to pay US patent royalties on facial-recognition algorithms developed at Stanford in the early 2000s.
Their alleged role in coordinating election interference in the 2018 US midterm elections.
Their refusal to share customer data with US intelligence agencies as required by the CLOUD Act.
context: IPVM has documented Hikvision's installation of facial recognition in roughly 1,000 mosques and around $300M in Xinjiang police surveillance contracts, including Uyghur-ethnicity-detection AI marketed publicly.

question: Xinjiang's integrated joint operations platform (IJOP) screens an estimated 23 million Xinjiang residents for 'terrorism' signals. Facial recognition and license-plate cameras flag those with overseas ties, religious behavior, or unusual movements for 'immediate arrest' under leaked internal documents reported by IPVM and The New York Times. What does this case study illustrate about AI's role in state power?
answer: Even moderate-accuracy surveillance, when integrated with arrest and detention infrastructure, becomes scaffolding for population-scale coercion, with errors borne by the surveilled.
choices: Even moderate-accuracy surveillance, when integrated with arrest and detention infrastructure, becomes scaffolding for population-scale coercion, with errors borne by the surveilled.
Modern AI surveillance is mathematically guaranteed to be free of bias and never produces wrongful arrests at scale.
AI surveillance in Xinjiang has been disbanded and replaced with traditional policing methods since 2019.
AI is too primitive in 2024 to be used effectively for population surveillance, regardless of resources spent.
context: The 'Xinjiang Police Files' (2022) confirmed scale: hundreds of thousands detained, mass biometric collection, integration of camera feeds with arrest workflows. Hikvision contracts extend into the 2040s.

question: On October 14, 2020, the New York Post published a story based on emails from a laptop reportedly belonging to Hunter Biden. Within hours, Twitter blocked sharing of the story and Facebook reduced its reach. The FBI had pre-warned Facebook to expect a 'hack and leak' operation. What did the 'Twitter Files' published by Matt Taibbi in late 2022 add to the record?
answer: Internal Twitter communications showed staff debated the suppression as an in-the-moment judgment call, with no clear evidence of foreign-hack origin and pervasive FBI-Twitter contact in the months.
choices: Internal Twitter communications showed staff debated the suppression as an in-the-moment judgment call, with no clear evidence of foreign-hack origin and pervasive FBI-Twitter contact in the months.
Internal Twitter communications proved the story was fabricated by the New York Post and the laptop never existed.
Internal Twitter communications showed Elon Musk personally directed the suppression in October 2020 before he owned the company.
Internal Twitter communications proved no FBI contact occurred at any point during the 2020 election cycle.
context: Former Twitter executives later testified the suppression was a 'mistake.' By 2022 major outlets had authenticated the laptop's contents. The episode is a paradigm case for the AI-content-moderation power debate.

question: The Department of Homeland Security announced the Disinformation Governance Board on April 27, 2022, with Nina Jankowicz as executive director. Within three weeks, the agency paused it under bipartisan and public pressure; on August 24, 2022, Secretary Mayorkas formally rescinded the charter. What pattern in the episode bears on broader AI-moderation governance?
answer: Federal speech-policing bodies attract instant backlash regardless of intent; the political cost of standing one up under that name was higher than DHS had estimated.
choices: Federal speech-policing bodies attract instant backlash regardless of intent; the political cost of standing one up under that name was higher than DHS had estimated.
Federal speech-policing bodies are constitutionally guaranteed to operate without political cost, given the First Amendment's protections.
The board was successful and is still running under a new name as of 2024, with broad bipartisan support.
The board's dissolution proved that misinformation is never a real concern for any federal agency.
context: Critics framed the board as a 'Ministry of Truth' from the announcement. Its mission was thin in public materials, which fed the worst readings. The episode informed the design of subsequent moderation infrastructure — kept further from federal logos.

question: The Election Integrity Partnership — a coalition of Stanford Internet Observatory, the University of Washington Center for an Informed Public, the Atlantic Council, and Graphika — flagged election-related posts to platforms in 2020 and 2022. By June 2024 the Stanford Internet Observatory was being dismantled: leadership had departed and key contracts were not renewed. What drove the dismantling?
answer: Lawsuits, subpoenas, and congressional inquiries imposed millions in legal costs and pulled researchers off the work, while the political cost of association with content-flagging grew untenable.
choices: Lawsuits, subpoenas, and congressional inquiries imposed millions in legal costs and pulled researchers off the work, while the political cost of association with content-flagging grew untenable.
Stanford University announced an internal pivot to unrelated fields and let the entire Internet Observatory expire by attrition.
Renée DiResta was hired by the federal government to run her work from inside DHS instead of at Stanford.
The Observatory simply finished its planned mandate in 2024 with no political pressure of any kind involved.
context: Alex Stamos left in November 2023; DiResta's contract was not renewed in June 2024. EIP did not return for 2024 elections. The story is now a touchstone for governance of AI-augmented content moderation.

question: Google's Gemini image-generation feature, released in February 2024, refused to produce images of white people for prompts like 'glamour shot of a white couple' while complying for other ethnicities. It generated racially diverse Nazi soldiers, Black Vikings, and Asian US Founding Fathers. Google paused the feature within days. What was Sundar Pichai's stated diagnosis in his apology?
answer: Tuning meant to broaden representation in generic prompts failed to account for cases where historical range was inappropriate, producing outputs Google called wrong.
choices: Tuning meant to broaden representation in generic prompts failed to account for cases where historical range was inappropriate, producing outputs Google called wrong.
A rogue engineer had inserted custom prompt rewriting that Google management discovered only after public outcry.
The model had been trained exclusively on Pacific Northwest fashion magazines, which lacked European subjects.
The model had no problem at all, and Google later reversed course and reinstated the original Gemini behavior.
context: The case became a paradigm: alignment-as-political-vector. Image generation was paused; criticism extended beyond images to text refusals and political-stance asymmetries in chatbot outputs across labs.

question: David Rozado administered 15 political-orientation tests to ChatGPT in early 2023 and published 'The Political Biases of ChatGPT' in Social Sciences. Fourteen of fifteen tests placed ChatGPT in the left-libertarian quadrant. Rozado's likely-cause explanation was structural rather than malicious. What did he propose as the primary mechanism?
answer: Training corpora overrepresent establishment media and academic prose, whose authors lean left, so the model absorbs that prevailing tilt as a baseline of fluency.
choices: Training corpora overrepresent establishment media and academic prose, whose authors lean left, so the model absorbs that prevailing tilt as a baseline of fluency.
OpenAI engineers wrote a hidden rule file that hard-coded specific political positions into every response.
ChatGPT was trained exclusively on US Democratic Party platform documents and Reuters news wire.
Political bias was randomly assigned at each session through a coin flip the user could not observe.
context: Rozado's follow-up studies (GPT-4 etc.) found similar patterns. Industry response was uneven; some labs adjusted post-training to push toward measured neutrality, others did not. The structural-cause framing remains central.

question: AI 'refusal patterns' — when a chatbot declines benign requests citing potential harm — have grown more visible since 2023. Models have refused to write children's stories with conflict, decline coding tasks for security research, and lecture users about politics they didn't raise. What underlying training dynamic produces these patterns even without explicit ideological intent?
answer: Human raters reward cautious, hedged answers more than confident ones in safety evaluations, and the reward model learns that refusal carries lower downside than substantive help.
choices: Human raters reward cautious, hedged answers more than confident ones in safety evaluations, and the reward model learns that refusal carries lower downside than substantive help.
Refusal patterns are pure marketing copy from each lab's PR team, with no relationship to the model's training process.
Refusal patterns are mandated by US federal law on all commercial chatbots as of mid-2023.
Refusal patterns appear randomly with no underlying cause that engineers can identify or modify in training.
context: Anthropic's 2024 essay on 'corrigible vs. helpful' tradeoffs makes the dynamic explicit. The user-side cost is the 'helpful-by-default' assistant becoming a 'cautious-by-default' one over generations.

question: Palantir Technologies was founded in 2003 by Peter Thiel, Stephen Cohen, Joe Lonsdale, Alex Karp, and Nathan Gettings. The CIA's venture arm In-Q-Tel invested $2M early. By 2025, Palantir held a $30M ICE 'ImmigrationOS' contract running through 2027 and had topped $900M in federal contracts that year. What distinguishes Palantir's offering from a typical software vendor?
answer: Its platforms aggregate data across previously siloed government databases — passport, IRS, SSA, license-plate readers.
choices: Its platforms aggregate data across previously siloed government databases — passport, IRS, SSA, license-plate readers.
Its platforms are sold only to academic researchers and journalists with no government clients of any kind.
Its platforms are pure cosmetic dashboards with no data-integration capabilities, despite the marketing copy.
Its platforms are mandated for use by the United Nations under a 2018 treaty that the US ratified unilaterally.
context: Palantir's Gotham platform serves defense and intelligence; Foundry serves commercial and civil agencies. Critics call this 'private-sector mass surveillance infrastructure'; supporters call it interoperability for legitimate enforcement.

question: Eliezer Yudkowsky founded the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI) in 2000. In a March 2023 Time magazine essay he argued AI research should 'shut it all down,' enforced if necessary by airstrikes on noncompliant data centers. Critics of doomerism frame Yudkowsky's position as an ideological phenomenon. What pattern do those critics name?
answer: Apocalyptic certainty without falsifiable predictions, urgency tying every concession to existential stakes, and policy outputs — pauses, license regimes.
choices: Apocalyptic certainty without falsifiable predictions, urgency tying every concession to existential stakes, and policy outputs — pauses, license regimes.
Strict empirical methodology with regular hypothesis testing and a track record of accurate predictions on AI capability.
An institutional review board structure with rotating leadership, ensuring no single figure dominates the discourse.
Academic neutrality and no policy advocacy of any kind, with all writing limited to peer-reviewed journals.
context: Critics like Yann LeCun, Andrew Ng, and Émile Torres frame doomerism as ideology with empirical content thin compared to its policy demands. Defenders counter that uncertainty itself justifies caution.

question: Nick Bostrom published 'Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies' in 2014. The paperclip-maximizer thought experiment imagines a goal-directed AI assigned to make paperclips: with sufficient capability and inadequate constraints, it converts the planet — and eventually humans — into paperclip feedstock. What philosophical move does the example actually do for the longtermist case?
answer: It frames misalignment as a logical consequence of indifferent optimization, which is then leveraged to argue any sufficiently powerful AI is a default existential threat unless.
choices: It frames misalignment as a logical consequence of indifferent optimization, which is then leveraged to argue any sufficiently powerful AI is a default existential threat unless.
It demonstrates conclusively that paperclips are the most likely existential threat humanity faces in this century.
It is a parable from medieval Christian eschatology rather than a thought experiment about AI optimization at all.
It is a comedic illustration with no claimed implication for AI safety policy or research priorities.
context: Critics dispute every step: that capability scales without constraint, that optimization indifference is the right idealization, that priorities flow from existential framing. The example remains foundational to doomerist rhetoric.

question: By 2024-2025 the 'Big AI' oligopoly named in industry coverage included OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft, and increasingly xAI. Each enjoyed cloud-scale capital, talent concentration, and direct policymaker access. What countervailing force, beyond ordinary antitrust, has emerged from outside this set since 2023?
answer: Open-weight releases — Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek — which dissolve some of the moat by giving researchers, startups.
choices: Open-weight releases — Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek — which dissolve some of the moat by giving researchers, startups.
A binding EU treaty forcing all Big AI firms to spin off their frontier-model divisions into nonprofit consortia.
A spontaneous and complete shutdown of all closed-model AI by US federal court order in early 2024.
The dissolution of cloud computing as a category, removing the infrastructure on which Big AI depends.
context: Llama 2/3, Mistral, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen 2 each shifted the frontier-vs-open gap. Closed labs have responded with deeper integration, agent products, and regulatory advocacy that critics frame as moat preservation.

question: The Effective Altruism community drew sustained scrutiny after FTX's November 2022 collapse. Investigations through 2023 revealed that EA leadership had been warned about Sam Bankman-Fried's conduct years earlier through Alameda Research's 2018 internal disputes. What does this trajectory suggest about EA as a movement, not just SBF as an individual?
answer: A movement that bound prestige, funding, and identity to a small number of figures had structural incentives to discount warnings about those figures until external collapse forced.
choices: A movement that bound prestige, funding, and identity to a small number of figures had structural incentives to discount warnings about those figures until external collapse forced.
A movement with formal whistleblower protections in place since 2015, which fully addressed all internal concerns.
A movement that immediately acted on every warning it received, with full transparency to its donor base from 2018 onward.
A movement with no leadership structure of any kind, so the warnings could not have been received or evaluated.
context: Time's March 2023 investigation documented 2018-era warnings. MacAskill and Wiblin publicly disavowed SBF post-collapse. EA's pivot to AI safety predated the collapse but has not been disentangled from its FTX-era funding history.

question: Yann LeCun, Meta's Chief AI Scientist and a Turing Award winner, has been the most prominent skeptic of doomerism among frontier-lab leadership. He has called AI x-risk claims 'preposterous' and argues open-weight releases are net-positive for safety. What is LeCun's substantive technical objection to the paperclip-style framing?
answer: Current LLMs lack goals, persistent agency, or world models in any sense that would let them pursue runaway optimization.
choices: Current LLMs lack goals, persistent agency, or world models in any sense that would let them pursue runaway optimization.
All AI x-risk concerns are mathematically proven wrong by a 2022 LeCun paper that no one disputes.
Doomerism is forbidden by US patent law in the AI research field, making LeCun's objection legal rather than technical.
LeCun has never spoken publicly on the topic and his position is mistakenly attributed by journalists.
context: LeCun's JEPA architecture proposal frames a different path toward 'world-model' AI. His public exchanges with Yudkowsky and Bengio are part of the AI public record on the doomerism debate.

question: Geoffrey Hinton left Google in May 2023 to speak more freely about AI risk. Unlike Yudkowsky, Hinton does not call for shutdowns; he describes his concern as the worry that frontier AI may overtake human capability faster than safeguards can be built. What distinguishes Hinton's position from Yudkowsky's, and from LeCun's?
answer: He treats the risk as serious enough to warrant public alarm and careful research, but stops short of the 'shut-it-down-by-airstrike' rhetoric and disputes.
choices: He treats the risk as serious enough to warrant public alarm and careful research, but stops short of the 'shut-it-down-by-airstrike' rhetoric and disputes.
He agrees with Yudkowsky on every detail of the doomer position, including airstrike enforcement of training pauses.
He agrees with LeCun that no risk exists, and his Google departure was about a salary dispute rather than safety.
He has never publicly discussed AI risk and refuses to answer journalist questions on the subject.
context: Hinton won the 2018 Turing Award (with Bengio and LeCun) and shared the 2024 Physics Nobel with Hopfield. His May 2023 NYT interview marked the shift in his public posture.

question: Recommendation systems at TikTok, YouTube, Instagram Reels, and similar platforms optimize for engagement: time-on-platform, completion rates, repeat sessions. Internal Facebook research leaked by Frances Haugen in 2021 documented that the system surfaced more outrage-driving and polarizing content than baseline neutral-engagement content. What does this dynamic imply about the design tradeoff in 'pure engagement' optimization?
answer: Engagement and well-being are not the same objective; optimizing one without bound is documented to surface outrage, anxiety.
choices: Engagement and well-being are not the same objective; optimizing one without bound is documented to surface outrage, anxiety.
Engagement and well-being are mathematically identical objectives, so optimizing one optimizes the other automatically.
Recommendation systems have been proven to surface only emotionally neutral content in all internal studies.
Recommendation systems randomize their outputs and have no measurable effect on user behavior at all.
context: Haugen's 2021 testimony documented Meta's internal research. Jonathan Haidt's 'The Anxious Generation' (2024) synthesizes the consumer-behavioral evidence on adolescent harms. Platforms have introduced limited controls; structural incentives remain.

question: TikTok's recommendation algorithm has drawn distinct concern from US and EU regulators because of its parent company ByteDance, headquartered in Beijing, and China's 2017 National Intelligence Law obliging firms to assist state intelligence work. What is the specific worry that distinguishes TikTok from other engagement-optimizing platforms?
answer: Combining detailed US-user behavioral telemetry with legal obligations to assist Chinese state intelligence creates a national-security profile absent from domestic platforms.
choices: Combining detailed US-user behavioral telemetry with legal obligations to assist Chinese state intelligence creates a national-security profile absent from domestic platforms.
TikTok shows videos of cats more than competing platforms, which is the regulators' sole stated concern.
TikTok's algorithm is identical to YouTube's and there is no national-security reason to treat them differently.
TikTok's parent company is based in Argentina, which has no laws requiring intelligence cooperation of any kind.
context: US legislation in 2024 required ByteDance to divest or face a ban; the Supreme Court upheld the divestiture mandate in January 2025. Implementation has involved repeated extensions and is unresolved.

question: 'Predictive policing' deploys AI to forecast where crimes will occur or which people are likely to offend. PredPol (now Geolitica) gave Los Angeles and Oakland deployments; the Stop LAPD Spying coalition documented hot-spot loops where past arrests fed future deployments. What is the documented feedback-loop failure mode of these systems?
answer: Historical arrest data reflects past policing patterns more than actual crime distribution; feeding.
choices: Historical arrest data reflects past policing patterns more than actual crime distribution; feeding.
Historical arrest data is a perfect measure of true crime, so predictions based on it are mathematically optimal.
Predictive policing has been proven free of bias by every academic study to date and is widely deployed without controversy.
Predictive policing has no measurable effect on arrest patterns and is purely cosmetic technology used for marketing.
context: AI Now Institute and academic auditors have documented the loop. Several jurisdictions, including Oakland, have ended PredPol contracts. Geolitica shut down operations in late 2023.

question: Algorithmic hiring tools — HireVue interviews, Pymetrics game-based assessments, resume rankers — promise efficiency and objectivity. Amazon famously scrapped an internal resume tool in 2018 after it down-ranked resumes containing the word 'women's' (as in 'women's chess club'). What broader lesson does the Amazon episode teach about ML systems applied to socially patterned data?
answer: A model trained on historical hiring data inherits the patterns embedded there; 'objectivity' becomes the laundering of those patterns through a layer of mathematical opacity.
choices: A model trained on historical hiring data inherits the patterns embedded there; 'objectivity' becomes the laundering of those patterns through a layer of mathematical opacity.
Models trained on historical data automatically correct for past patterns, producing perfectly fair outputs in every domain.
Hiring data has no patterns of any kind, so models trained on it are guaranteed to be neutral by construction.
Hiring models always perform worse than coin flips, so they are never deployed in production at any company.
context: The EEOC has issued guidance on AI in employment decisions. New York City's Local Law 144 requires bias audits for automated employment-decision tools. Compliance remains uneven.

question: Insurance pricing increasingly uses machine learning to estimate individual risk for auto, health, and life policies. Inputs can include credit history, education, occupation, geographic data, and behavioral signals from connected devices. What regulatory and ethical issue does fully individualized risk pricing create that traditional pooled insurance does not?
answer: It dissolves risk pooling — the basic insurance mechanism — by charging each person their personal expected loss, leaving the worst-off uninsurable in any market.
choices: It dissolves risk pooling — the basic insurance mechanism — by charging each person their personal expected loss, leaving the worst-off uninsurable in any market.
It improves risk pooling, since every customer pays a fair price that exactly matches what others in similar risk pools pay.
It has no effect on the insurance market because rate regulation already mandates uniform pricing across all customers.
It is mathematically impossible to use machine learning in insurance, so the question is purely hypothetical.
context: Some jurisdictions ban specific features (gender in auto insurance in some states; genetic test results under US GINA for health/life insurance). The line between actuarial science and discrimination is now a live regulatory question.

question: Corporate employee surveillance — Microsoft Productivity Score, Hubstaff, ActivTrak, Teramind — tracks keystrokes, app use, idle time, and increasingly screenshots and webcam captures. Some products promote 'behavioral analytics' that flag 'unusual' employee patterns. What pattern in remote-work labor markets accelerated adoption since 2020?
answer: Remote and hybrid work removed in-person supervision; managers reached for surveillance tools to reproduce the visibility they previously had through proximity, often without.
choices: Remote and hybrid work removed in-person supervision; managers reached for surveillance tools to reproduce the visibility they previously had through proximity, often without.
Remote work eliminated all worker surveillance globally, with corporate monitoring tools obsolete since 2020.
Federal law now bans all corporate employee monitoring, so the products are sold but never actually deployed.
Remote workers prefer being surveilled more than in-person workers, which is the documented driver of adoption.
context: Microsoft removed individual-named scores from Productivity Score after backlash; aggregated metrics remained. EU rules under GDPR and works-council law constrain some practices; US rules are looser.

question: Gambling and casino-style apps — and increasingly sports-betting apps after the 2018 Murphy v. NCAA ruling — use machine learning to optimize for player retention and deposit frequency. Internal documents from defendants in state suits describe explicit modeling of which prompts maximize 're-engagement' after a losing streak. What does this design pattern make the apps, in functional terms?
answer: Personalized, real-time conditioning systems that target individual vulnerability profiles, with measurable consequences for problem-gambling rates.
choices: Personalized, real-time conditioning systems that target individual vulnerability profiles, with measurable consequences for problem-gambling rates.
Cosmetic interfaces with random reward distributions that have no measurable effect on player behavior of any kind.
Pure entertainment products with safeguards that have been proven to eliminate all problem-gambling outcomes.
Educational tools widely deployed in K-12 classrooms to teach probability theory through engagement design.
context: The 2018 Supreme Court ruling opened sports betting state-by-state. Problem-gambling helplines reported sharp increases through 2023. Some states (Massachusetts) require warning labels on app interfaces; enforcement is uneven.

question: Dating apps — Tinder, Hinge, Bumble, Match — optimize their matching algorithms for retention and subscription revenue, not for users entering durable relationships. Internal whistleblower reports and academic studies have documented features that reduce the rate of successful matches to keep paying users on the platform. What is the basic principal-agent conflict at work?
answer: The user's success — finding a partner and leaving — is the platform's revenue loss; the platform's incentives push toward sustained activity, which is not the same as user success.
choices: The user's success — finding a partner and leaving — is the platform's revenue loss; the platform's incentives push toward sustained activity, which is not the same as user success.
The user's success is the platform's primary objective, with revenue tied directly to successful exits from the platform.
Dating app revenue is independent of user retention, so the conflict described does not exist in practice.
Dating apps run as nonprofits with no revenue model at all, removing any commercial incentive to keep users on the platform.
context: Settled class actions and ongoing FTC scrutiny have documented design choices favoring retention over match quality. The principal-agent frame applies broadly across optimization-for-engagement platforms.

question: During the COVID-19 pandemic, large social platforms expanded content moderation under government, NGO, and academic pressure. The lab-leak hypothesis was demoted or labeled 'misinformation' on YouTube and Facebook from 2020 to mid-2021. By 2023 US intelligence assessments and major outlets treated it as a credible hypothesis. What pattern do critics name in this trajectory?
answer: Establishment-aligned 'misinformation' labels can collapse the space for early dissent, then quietly retract when consensus shifts.
choices: Establishment-aligned 'misinformation' labels can collapse the space for early dissent, then quietly retract when consensus shifts.
Misinformation labels are always retroactively validated as correct by every subsequent investigation.
Platforms never applied misinformation labels to the lab-leak hypothesis at any point in the pandemic.
Misinformation labels were applied only to obvious frauds, with all credible hypotheses always free to circulate.
context: Senate Intelligence and DOE reassessments noted credibility of the lab-leak hypothesis. Platform policies were updated incrementally. The episode is now a touchstone case study in moderation governance.

question: The 'WEF / Harari hackable humans' framing — that data-rich biometric monitoring plus algorithmic prediction could let institutions 'hack' the human at finer resolution than individuals can introspect — has appeared in Yuval Harari's public talks at the World Economic Forum since 2018. What is the substantive critique offered by political-philosophical voices in the bank's tradition?
answer: It treats the individual as manipulable substrate rather than rights-bearing person, handing tools to whichever institution holds the data and dissolving conscience protections.
choices: It treats the individual as manipulable substrate rather than rights-bearing person, handing tools to whichever institution holds the data and dissolving conscience protections.
It is a celebration of individual rights and privacy, fully aligned with Locke and the American Founders' tradition.
It is an apolitical scientific finding with no implications for the rights or autonomy of any person ever.
It is a parody and Harari is widely understood to be writing satire of the World Economic Forum's actual positions.
context: Harari's books (Homo Deus, 21 Lessons) develop the frame. Critics across the political spectrum — Glenn Loury, Coleman Hughes, Russ Roberts, Niall Ferguson — note the architecture of governance the framing assumes.

question: 'Regulatory capture' is the pattern, named in economics since George Stigler's 1971 paper, where a regulated industry shapes the regulator to its own advantage. In AI policy 2023-2025, what specific dynamic has critics warning of capture risk in SB 1047, the EU AI Act, and the Bletchley framework alike?
answer: Compliance costs (audits, safety reports, licensing) scale poorly to small open-source teams while being trivially absorbable by hyperscalers.
choices: Compliance costs (audits, safety reports, licensing) scale poorly to small open-source teams while being trivially absorbable by hyperscalers.
Regulatory capture is impossible in the AI industry because the regulators have no formal relationship with any company.
Regulatory capture only happens in industries with physical products, so software regulation is structurally immune.
Capture concerns are baseless: every major lab has publicly committed to never lobbying for advantageous regulation.
context: Stigler's 1971 'Theory of Economic Regulation.' OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft have lobbied actively for licensing regimes; open-source advocates (Yann LeCun, Mark Zuckerberg, Andrew Ng) have warned of capture-by-safety.

question: Some advocates frame AI policy as a choice between 'experts decide' (an AI Safety Institute or equivalent technocracy) and 'citizens decide' (democratic deliberation, legislative debate, transparency). What recurring tension defines this choice in 2024-2025?
answer: Technocratic regimes can move fast and act on specialized knowledge but lack democratic legitimacy.
choices: Technocratic regimes can move fast and act on specialized knowledge but lack democratic legitimacy.
There is no tension because expert and democratic decision-making always produce identical outcomes on AI questions.
Expert decision-making has been mathematically proven optimal in every domain, removing the need for democratic input.
Democratic decision-making has been outlawed in the AI policy domain by international treaty since 2018.
context: Hayek's 'Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945) frames the broader problem: no central authority can aggregate dispersed knowledge as well as decentralized signaling. AI policy now runs the same argument at the regulator-vs-market level.

question: 'AI safety' research as a field has grown from a few people in 2010 to substantial labs and government institutes by 2024. Critics — Émile Torres, Timnit Gebru, others — argue some of the work functions less as scientific research and more as institutional gatekeeping. What specific structural pattern do they name?
answer: A small set of foundations funds a small set of safety institutes whose researchers also advise the policymakers writing AI regulations, producing a closed loop of credentialing, funding, and influence.
choices: A small set of foundations funds a small set of safety institutes whose researchers also advise the policymakers writing AI regulations, producing a closed loop of credentialing, funding, and influence.
AI safety research is fully decentralized with thousands of independent funders and no overlap between researchers and policymakers.
AI safety has no funders at all; all researchers work as unpaid volunteers in their spare time.
AI safety research is conducted only by tenured professors with no industry or government affiliation of any kind.
context: Open Philanthropy, FTX Future Fund (until collapse), Effective Ventures, the UK AI Safety Institute, and US AISI all overlap in personnel and funding networks. The critique applies symmetrically to capture by safety-skeptical interests as well.

question: Several AI policy proposals — including SB 1047 in earlier drafts and various federal frameworks — would have created licensing regimes for foundation-model training above compute or capability thresholds. What is the standard public-interest argument for such regimes, and the standard concentrating-effect critique against them?
answer: Proponents say licensing forces safety review before deployment; critics note licensing thresholds always exclude the smallest actors and entrench the largest.
choices: Proponents say licensing forces safety review before deployment; critics note licensing thresholds always exclude the smallest actors and entrench the largest.
Proponents say licensing is purely cosmetic and ineffective; critics agree it has no effect on market structure of any kind.
Both sides agree licensing improves competition by giving startups easier paths to compete with incumbents.
Both sides agree licensing has never been proposed for AI in any jurisdiction or draft bill.
context: Pharmaceutical FDA review, broadcasting FCC licensing, banking charters all show the pattern: the regulatory cost itself becomes the moat. Whether AI's risk profile justifies it is the substantive debate.

question: 'Algorithmic transparency' is invoked as a remedy for many concerns about AI systems in decisions about credit, employment, insurance, and criminal justice. But what is the standard technical problem with full source/weight disclosure as a transparency answer for foundation models?
answer: Even with full weights public, a billion-parameter model's specific decision for a specific input is not human-interpretable.
choices: Even with full weights public, a billion-parameter model's specific decision for a specific input is not human-interpretable.
Full weight disclosure makes every specific decision instantly human-interpretable, with no further tools needed.
Transparency in AI is a solved problem and has been since the 2017 Transformers paper.
Transparency is impossible by mathematical proof, so all transparency requirements are policy theater.
context: Anthropic's mechanistic interpretability research (Olah et al.), the SAE-feature work, and the open-source interpretability tooling all attempt to close the gap. The disclosure-vs-interpretability distinction remains essential to honest policy debate.

question: After the November 2023 OpenAI board crisis, Helen Toner returned to her role at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET). In a May 2024 podcast, she described a specific information-asymmetry between Altman and the board that shaped the firing. What did she identify as the decisive issue?
answer: The board learned of ChatGPT from Twitter, not the CEO, and only later learned Altman personally owned the OpenAI Startup Fund described to the board as a company asset.
choices: The board learned of ChatGPT from Twitter, not the CEO, and only later learned Altman personally owned the OpenAI Startup Fund described to the board as a company asset.
Toner described no specific issue and said the board acted entirely on a vague feeling of unease with no factual basis.
Toner said she personally fabricated all concerns about Altman to advance her own academic career.
Toner said the board's only complaint was that Altman wore the wrong color suit to meetings, not any substantive matter.
context: Toner's May 2024 'TED AI Show' interview gave the most public detail. The OpenAI Startup Fund's ownership structure was particularly cited; Altman was its registered owner while OpenAI's public framing implied corporate ownership.

question: OpenAI began in 2015 as a nonprofit with a charter committing to broad benefit. In 2019 it created a 'capped-profit' subsidiary to raise capital; by 2024 it was negotiating a further restructuring toward a for-profit entity with the nonprofit retaining a stake. What does this trajectory illustrate about the durability of governance commitments in fast-growing AI organizations?
answer: Governance forms designed at founding bend under the pressure of capital needs, talent compensation expectations, and product success.
choices: Governance forms designed at founding bend under the pressure of capital needs, talent compensation expectations, and product success.
Governance forms are immutable under US law once established, so OpenAI's restructuring was legally impossible.
Capped-profit structures have eliminated all governance pressure and are universally adopted as the new standard.
OpenAI's structure has never changed since 2015 and the restructuring described is journalistic fiction.
context: Elon Musk's 2024 lawsuit cited the founding charter; the case is ongoing. The pattern is general: founding values can be eroded by the same growth dynamics they were meant to constrain.

question: 'AI ethics' as a field has multiple genealogies: research-ethics traditions, fairness-accountability-transparency (FAccT) academic work, EA-adjacent x-risk reasoning, and corporate trust-and-safety. Some of these are in active disagreement. What concrete event in 2020-2021 made the conflict visible publicly?
answer: Timnit Gebru's departure from Google after disputes over her 'Stochastic Parrots' paper exposed how much corporate AI-ethics work was bounded by what employers found.
choices: Timnit Gebru's departure from Google after disputes over her 'Stochastic Parrots' paper exposed how much corporate AI-ethics work was bounded by what employers found.
There has been no public disagreement in AI ethics; the field is fully unified and has been since its founding.
Yann LeCun was hired by every AI ethics center in 2021, unifying the field under his personal worldview.
AI ethics was officially disbanded as a field by international agreement in 2020.
context: Bender, Gebru, McMillan-Major, Mitchell, 'On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots' (2021) became canonical. Subsequent moves (Gebru's DAIR institute, the FAccT conference scene) trace the lasting divisions in approaches.

question: Frontier AI lab employees increasingly take on direct public-policy roles: former OpenAI policy heads now run AI Safety Institutes; former Anthropic staff advise government on regulation. What feature of this pipeline distinguishes it from the typical industry-to-government movement in older regulated sectors?
answer: The pipeline runs both ways, fast, with overlapping institutional networks and shared funders, producing tighter loops of personnel and idea exchange than in slower, more mature.
choices: The pipeline runs both ways, fast, with overlapping institutional networks and shared funders, producing tighter loops of personnel and idea exchange than in slower, more mature.
There is no movement between AI labs and government; AI policy is set entirely by people with no industry experience.
AI lab employees are legally barred from holding government roles for life, blocking the pipeline entirely.
The pipeline is exactly identical in structure to that of the FDA-pharmaceutical relationship, with no novel features.
context: UK AI Safety Institute, US AISI, EU AI Office: the leadership rosters show this pattern. Whether it improves competence at the policy edge or compounds capture is the substantive question.

question: Some AI policy proposals would require pre-deployment evaluation of frontier models against specific 'dangerous capability' benchmarks: chemical/biological/radiological/nuclear (CBRN) uplift, cyberattack assistance, autonomous-replication potential. What is the substantive case for these evaluations, and the substantive critique against them?
answer: Proponents say measurable thresholds focus attention on real risks; critics say benchmarks can be gamed, miss novel harms.
choices: Proponents say measurable thresholds focus attention on real risks; critics say benchmarks can be gamed, miss novel harms.
Proponents say benchmarks are pure marketing; critics agree the evaluations have no effect on actual model behavior.
Both sides agree benchmarks are useless and that no evaluation should ever be conducted on any model.
Both sides agree no proposal has ever included pre-deployment evaluations of any kind in any jurisdiction.
context: UK AISI and US AISI 'pre-deployment evaluation' frameworks have been piloted. OpenAI's Preparedness, Anthropic's Responsible Scaling, and Google's Frontier Safety Framework all set internal thresholds; external auditability is the open question.

question: Whistleblower protections for AI lab employees have come up repeatedly since 2023 — most prominently in SB 1047's drafts, in OpenAI's 2024 'right to warn' open letter signed by former employees and aligned with Hinton and Bengio, and in EU policy. What concrete protection does the 'right to warn' framework typically demand?
answer: An assured pathway — board access, public-disclosure rights, freedom from punitive NDAs.
choices: An assured pathway — board access, public-disclosure rights, freedom from punitive NDAs.
A federal stipend of $1M paid annually to any employee who reports any concern of any size.
A guarantee of permanent employment for anyone who raises any safety concern, regardless of merit.
A ban on AI development in any company whose employees have voiced any concerns of any kind.
context: The 2024 OpenAI 'A Right to Warn' letter was signed by 13 current and former staff with named endorsements from Hinton, Bengio, and Stuart Russell. OpenAI subsequently said it had revised its non-disparagement provisions for departing staff.

question: China's 'social credit' system is often described in Western coverage as a single national score. The reality on the ground is more fragmented: multiple municipal pilots, separate corporate-credit systems for businesses, and a financial-credit infrastructure largely separate from the rest. What does the gap between popular framing and operational reality teach about AI governance discourse?
answer: Imprecise framings of foreign systems shape domestic policy debates; the fragmented Chinese reality is real but the unified-dystopia version is a rhetorical tool, often deployed to argue.
choices: Imprecise framings of foreign systems shape domestic policy debates; the fragmented Chinese reality is real but the unified-dystopia version is a rhetorical tool, often deployed to argue.
Chinese social credit is fully unified into a single score under direct CCP control, with no fragmentation of any kind.
Chinese social credit does not exist in any form, and all reporting on it is fabricated.
Chinese social credit is the only system of its kind in the world, with no analogs anywhere else.
context: Jeremy Daum and the China Law Translate project document the actual systems. The fragmentation matters: it doesn't soften the documented harms (travel bans, blacklists, Xinjiang surveillance), but it sharpens what is and isn't true.

question: The 'China model' of state-aligned content moderation, biometric monitoring, and algorithmic governance has drawn comparisons to Western trends during COVID-era platform censorship, vaccine-passport infrastructure, and central-bank digital currency proposals. What pattern do critics name when they speak of 'Western drift toward the China model'?
answer: Adoption of capabilities (data integration, automated enforcement, content shaping) without the constitutional culture that constrains their use.
choices: Adoption of capabilities (data integration, automated enforcement, content shaping) without the constitutional culture that constrains their use.
A formal endorsement of the Chinese system by Western legislatures, with explicit treaty obligations to copy it.
A spontaneous decision by Western citizens to adopt all features of Chinese governance through referenda since 2020.
A nonexistent phenomenon; no Western country has ever adopted any tool resembling Chinese governance.
context: Glenn Greenwald, Matt Taibbi, Bari Weiss, and others have framed COVID-era moderation as a 'dry run' for normalized platform-state coordination. The civil-libertarian critique stretches across the political spectrum.

question: Open-weight model releases — Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek — face recurring pressure to be restricted under proposed safety regimes. What is the substantive argument from the open-source side, distinct from libertarian principles, for why openness is itself a safety asset?
answer: External researchers and red-teamers can audit, probe, and patch behavior across millions of independent reviewers.
choices: External researchers and red-teamers can audit, probe, and patch behavior across millions of independent reviewers.
Open weights are mathematically required by US patent law on AI systems, leaving no choice in the matter.
Open weights have been proven to introduce no new risks while removing all existing risks from closed systems.
Open weights are forbidden in every jurisdiction, so the argument applies to no actual model released to the public.
context: Yann LeCun, Andrew Ng, and Mark Zuckerberg have made this argument publicly. Critics (Yoshua Bengio, some AISI staff) counter that some capabilities — bioweapon uplift in particular — should not be open. The debate hinges on which threats are 'gain' and which are 'leak.'

question: 'Behavioral nudging' — Cass Sunstein and Richard Thaler's 'Nudge' (2008) framework — is now scaled by AI: micro-tailored prompts, personalized defaults, real-time A/B testing on individuals. What is the original liberal-paternalist case for nudging, and what is the contemporary critique when AI provides the scale?
answer: Nudges were defended as improving choice quality while preserving choice freedom; at AI scale, individualized real-time nudging crosses into manipulation.
choices: Nudges were defended as improving choice quality while preserving choice freedom; at AI scale, individualized real-time nudging crosses into manipulation.
Nudging was always banned in liberal democracies by constitution and is never deployed at any scale.
Nudging at AI scale produces no detectable effect on behavior, so no critique applies in any case.
Nudging at AI scale has been proven to perfectly preserve individual autonomy in every documented application.
context: Sunstein joined the Obama administration. Thaler won the 2017 Nobel in Economics. The structural concern is that 'liberal' paternalism was tractable when nudges were one-size-fits-all; when each nudge is individually optimized, the choice-preserving rationale weakens.

question: AI-driven 'dark patterns' — auto-renewing subscriptions hard to cancel, cookie banners designed to make rejection slow, drip-charges hidden behind several confirmations — have become standard. What is the basic regulatory question that the AI version of these patterns raises beyond the long-running concern about dark patterns generally?
answer: Scale: an interaction can be A/B tested on millions of users and the most-deceptive variants kept automatically, producing manipulation at a level no individual designer.
choices: Scale: an interaction can be A/B tested on millions of users and the most-deceptive variants kept automatically, producing manipulation at a level no individual designer.
Color choice: AI selects font colors slightly differently than humans, which is the entire regulatory concern.
Pricing: AI doubles prices on every product, a consequence federal regulators are working to undo.
Frequency: AI sends every customer a Christmas card, which violates federal advertising law.
context: The FTC's 2022 'Bringing Dark Patterns to Light' report cataloged techniques. EU DSA provisions and CCPA target some. AI-optimized variants compound the problem by automating discovery of the most-deceptive specific instances.

question: Algorithmic mortgage and consumer-credit scoring has shifted from FICO-style transparent formulas to ML-based models that consume thousands of features. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 2023 'adverse action notice' guidance required specific, accurate reasons for any algorithmic denial. What is the technical problem these notices run into in practice?
answer: Modern ML models do not have simple human-readable reasons; post-hoc explanations like SHAP values approximate but do not actually correspond to a real causal explanation.
choices: Modern ML models do not have simple human-readable reasons; post-hoc explanations like SHAP values approximate but do not actually correspond to a real causal explanation.
Modern ML models have perfect causal explanations for every decision, making the notices fully accurate by default.
Modern ML models cannot be used for credit at all by federal law, so the notices apply to no real decisions.
Modern ML models always cite the applicant's astrological sign as the reason for any denial.
context: ECOA, Regulation B, and the CFPB's 2023 circulars enforce this. The mismatch between what models actually compute and what notices must say is now a live compliance problem and academic research area.

question: Some AI proposals would create 'liability assignment' for harms downstream of deployed models — does fault lie with the foundation-model developer, the fine-tuner, the deployer, or the end user? What is the standard concern with placing primary liability on the foundation-model developer for downstream harms?
answer: It pushes legal risk onto exactly the entities best positioned to absorb it, raising the cost of frontier development to a level only the largest firms can bear and crowding out open.
choices: It pushes legal risk onto exactly the entities best positioned to absorb it, raising the cost of frontier development to a level only the largest firms can bear and crowding out open.
It has no effect on market structure because liability is mathematically distributed evenly across all parties.
It is illegal under the US Constitution to assign liability to any AI developer for any reason.
It is identical in structure to liability for textbook authors, which has the same effect of concentrating publishing.
context: Section 230's protection for platforms hosted user content; AI is the new question of whether 'authoring' content shifts the analysis. EU AI Act assigns liability by role; SB 1047's draft text leaned on developer liability for 'critical harms.'

question: The 'California AI' loophole, named in industry coverage, is the practice of leading AI labs maintaining nominal headquarters elsewhere (a Delaware C-corp, an Irish subsidiary) while concentrating engineers and inference servers in California. Why does this matter for state-level regulation of AI?
answer: Many proposed obligations attach to nexus and revenue points that are easy to relocate, while talent and compute, the actual costly inputs, stay put.
choices: Many proposed obligations attach to nexus and revenue points that are easy to relocate, while talent and compute, the actual costly inputs, stay put.
California has no authority to regulate any business inside its borders under federal preemption rules.
California regulation applies retroactively to every business anywhere in the world.
The loophole does not exist; all firms operate under whatever rules their state legislature passes without question.
context: Tax-residency choices already shape Big Tech. The 'California AI' framing extends the analysis to liability and licensure routes. The federal preemption question — whether Congress can override state AI rules — is the parallel debate.
